_**Los Olvidados**_ (Spanish:[[los olβiˈðaðos]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _**The Forgotten Ones**_; known in the United States as _**The Young and the Damned**_) is a 1950 [Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Mexico "Cinema of Mexico")[teen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_film "Teen film")[crime film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_film "Crime film") directed by Luis Buñuel. It was filmed at Tepeyac Studios and on location in Mexico City.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-2)

Producer Óscar Dancigers sought Buñuel to direct following the success of _[El Gran Calavera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Gran\_Calavera "El Gran Calavera")_ (1949). Buñuel already had a script ready titled _¡Mi huerfanito jefe!_ about a boy who sells lottery tickets. However, Dancigers had in mind a more realistic and serious depiction of children in poverty in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City"). After conducting research, Jesús Camacho and Buñuel came up with a script that Dancigers was pleased with. The film can be seen in the tradition of [social realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_realism "Social realism"), although it also contains elements of [surrealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") present in much of Buñuel's work.

While widely criticized upon initial release, _Los olvidados_ received [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Director_Award_(Cannes_Film_Festival) "Best Director Award (Cannes Film Festival)") at the [1951 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951_Cannes_Film_Festival "1951 Cannes Film Festival").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-3) It is now considered as one of the greatest and most influential films of all time.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

The film is about a group of destitute children and their misfortunes in a [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City") slum. El Jaibo escapes [juvenile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolescence "Adolescence") jail and reunites with the street gang that he leads. They attempt to rob a [blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blindness "Blindness")[street musician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_musician "Street musician") and, failing at first, later track him down, beat him, and destroy his instruments.

With the help of Pedro, El Jaibo tracks down Julián, the youngster who supposedly sent him to jail. El Jaibo puts his unharmed arm in a sling, hides a rock in it and confronts Julián, who denies that he reported him to the police and refuses to fight El Jaibo because it would not be a fair fight. As Julián starts to walk away, El Jaibo hits him in the back of the head with the rock. He then beats Julián to death with a stick and takes his money. El Jaibo warns Pedro not to report the crime and shares Julián's money with Pedro to make him an [accomplice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accomplice "Accomplice").

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Los_olvidados_U.S._still_%281950%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Los_olvidados_U.S._still_%281950%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Los_olvidados_U.S._still_(1950)_(cropped).jpg)

[Alfonso Mejía](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Mej%C3%ADa "Alfonso Mejía") as Pedro (right, behind) in a publicity photo for the film

Pedro's mother resents her son's behavior, and shows that she doesn't love or care for him. Pedro is saddened by this, vows to start behaving better and finds work as apprentice to a blacksmith. One day, El Jaibo comes to talk with him about their secret and, unbeknownst to Pedro, steals a customer's knife from the blacksmith's table. Pedro is accused of the crime and sent to a juvenile rehabilitation program, the "farm school", where he gets into a fight and kills two chickens. The principal tests Pedro by handing Pedro a 50 [pesos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_peso "Mexican peso") bill to run errands with. Pedro accepts and leaves with the intention to complete the errands. As soon as he leaves, he encounters El Jaibo, who steals the money. Upset that his attempt to be good was foiled again, Pedro tracks down El Jaibo and fights him. The fight ends in a stalemate, but Pedro announces to the crowd that it was El Jaibo who killed Julián. El Jaibo flees, but the blind man has heard the accusation and tells the police.

Pedro tracks El Jaibo down once again to murder him. El Jaibo [kills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_murder "Child murder") Pedro. While fleeing, El Jaibo encounters the police and, as he tries to run away, the police shoot and kill him. Meche and her grandfather find Pedro's body in their shed. Not wanting to get involved, they dump his body down a garbage-covered cliff. On their way, they pass Pedro's mother, who, though once unconcerned with her disobedient child, is now searching for him.

## Alternate ending

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Alternate ending")]

In 2002, it was announced that an alternate ending for _Los Olvidados_ (labeled "the happy ending") was discovered at the Film Warehouse of the [National Autonomous University of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Autonomous_University_of_Mexico "National Autonomous University of Mexico"), and it would be restored digitally in order to show it to the public. On 8 July 2005, it was rescreened with the alternate ending in a few selected venues and included in subsequent DVD releases.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-5)

At the International Cinematographic Festival in Saltillo, Coahuila, Mexico, on 3 February 2011, the last surviving member of the cast, Alfonso Mejía (Pedro), introduced the alternative ending to the film.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-6)

The alternative ending begins with El Jaibo and Pedro fighting in an abandoned warehouse. Pedro pushes El Jaibo from the roof, where he falls to his death. Pedro frisks the body for the money El Jaibo stole from him (in contrast to the original ending, where Pedro is murdered by El Jaibo). Pedro returns to the farm school with the money that the principal entrusted to him.

## Analysis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Analysis")]

Thematically, _Los Olvidados_ is similar to Buñuel's earlier Spanish film, _[Land Without Bread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land\_Without\_Bread "Land Without Bread")_. Both films deal with the never-ending [cycle of poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_of_poverty "Cycle of poverty") and despair. _Los Olvidados_ is especially interesting because although "Buñuel employed [...] elements of [Italian neorealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_neorealism "Italian neorealism")", a concurrent movement across the Atlantic Ocean marked by "outdoor locations, nonprofessional actors, low budget productions, and a focus on the working classes", _Los Olvidados_ is not a neorealist film (Fernandez, 42). "Neorealist reality is incomplete, conventional, and above all rational", Buñuel wrote in a 1953 essay titled "Poetry and Cinema". "The poetry, the mystery, all that completes and enlarges tangible reality is utterly lacking" (Sklar, 324). _Los Olvidados_ contains such surrealistic shots as when "a boy throws an egg at the camera lens, where it shatters and drips" or a scene in which a boy has a dream in slow-motion (Sklar, 324). The surrealist dream sequence was actually shot in reverse and switched in post-production. Buñuel does not romanticize the characters, and even the abused blind man is revealed to have cruel habits of preying on children and selling fake elixirs. Film historian Carl J. Mora has said of Los olvidados that the director "visualized poverty in a radically different way from the traditional forms of Mexican melodrama. Buñuel's street children are not 'ennobled' by their desperate struggle for survival; they are in fact ruthless predators who are not better than their equally unromanticized victims".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-mora-9)

## Controversy about possible plagiarism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Controversy about possible plagiarism")]

Journalist Verónica Calderón, in an article published on 14 August 2010 in the Spanish newspaper [El País](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Pa%C3%ADs "El País"), collects statements by Morelia Guerrero, daughter of Mexican journalist and writer Jesús R. Guerrero ([Numarán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numar%C3%A1n "Numarán"), [Michoacán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michoac%C3%A1n "Michoacán"), 1911–1979), in which Morelia points out that the script and the film are based on a novel written by her father, entitled _Los Olvidados_, published in 1944, with a prologue by Mexican writer [José Revueltas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Revueltas "José Revueltas"). The [National Polytechnic Institute of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Polytechnic_Institute_of_Mexico "National Polytechnic Institute of Mexico") (IPN) published, in December 2009, a second edition of the novel penned by Jesús R. Guerrero.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-10) However, comparative studies have been made between the film and the novel, and no trace of any plagiarism by Buñuel has been found.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-11)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Initial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Initial")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Los_olvidados_U.S._still_%281950%29_2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Los_olvidados_U.S._still_%281950%29_2_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Los_olvidados_U.S._still_(1950)_2_(cropped).jpg)

Mario Ramírez and [Roberto Cobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Cobo "Roberto Cobo") (right) in a publicity still for the film

_Los Olvidados_ was largely disparaged by the Mexican press upon its release.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-12) Juan Carlos Ibáñez and Manuel Palacio write, "The film was so harsh and innovative, so critical and daring in its statements that during its first screenings, spectators openly aired their indignation towards the features of Mexican identity presented by Buñuel."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-13) The work was also criticized as overly bleak.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-14)

Critic for _The New Yorker,_ Pauline Kael wrote that in _Los Olvidados_ "Buñuel makes you understand the pornography of brutality: the pornography is in what human beings are capable of doing to other human beings."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-15)

### Retrospective

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Retrospective")]

Many critics have since proclaimed _Los Olvidados_ a masterpiece. On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 91% of 43 critics' reviews are positive. The website's consensus reads: "_Los Olvidados_ casts an unsparing eye on juvenile crime -- and the systemically flawed societies that allow it to flourish."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-16) It was inscribed on [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s [Memory of the World International Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_of_the_World_International_Register "Memory of the World International Register") in 2003 in recognition of its historical significance.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-18)

The work placed 110th in the 2012 _[Sight & Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sight\_&\_Sound "Sight & Sound")_ critics' poll of the greatest films ever made.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-19) In April 2019, a restored version of the film was selected to be shown in the Cannes Classics section at the [2019 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Cannes_Film_Festival "2019 Cannes Film Festival").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-20) The film is ranked number 2 in the list of the best 100 Mexican films of all time according to 25 cinema critics (1994/2020).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-21)

## Influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Influence")]

_Los Olvidados_ has been cited as an influence on films such as _[Pixote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixote "Pixote")_ (1980), _[Amores perros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amores\_perros "Amores perros")_ (2000), and _[City of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City\_of\_God\_(2002\_film) "City of God (2002 film)")_ (2002).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-22)

_**Los Olvidados**_ (Spanish:[[los olβiˈðaðos]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _**The Forgotten Ones**_; known in the United States as _**The Young and the Damned**_) is a 1950 [Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Mexico "Cinema of Mexico")[teen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_film "Teen film")[crime film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_film "Crime film") directed by Luis Buñuel. It was filmed at Tepeyac Studios and on location in Mexico City.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-2)

Producer Óscar Dancigers sought Buñuel to direct following the success of _[El Gran Calavera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Gran\_Calavera "El Gran Calavera")_ (1949). Buñuel already had a script ready titled _¡Mi huerfanito jefe!_ about a boy who sells lottery tickets. However, Dancigers had in mind a more realistic and serious depiction of children in poverty in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City"). After conducting research, Jesús Camacho and Buñuel came up with a script that Dancigers was pleased with. The film can be seen in the tradition of [social realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_realism "Social realism"), although it also contains elements of [surrealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") present in much of Buñuel's work.

While widely criticized upon initial release, _Los olvidados_ received [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Director_Award_(Cannes_Film_Festival) "Best Director Award (Cannes Film Festival)") at the [1951 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951_Cannes_Film_Festival "1951 Cannes Film Festival").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-3) It is now considered as one of the greatest and most influential films of all time.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

The film is about a group of destitute children and their misfortunes in a [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City") slum. El Jaibo escapes [juvenile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolescence "Adolescence") jail and reunites with the street gang that he leads. They attempt to rob a [blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blindness "Blindness")[street musician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_musician "Street musician") and, failing at first, later track him down, beat him, and destroy his instruments.

With the help of Pedro, El Jaibo tracks down Julián, the youngster who supposedly sent him to jail. El Jaibo puts his unharmed arm in a sling, hides a rock in it and confronts Julián, who denies that he reported him to the police and refuses to fight El Jaibo because it would not be a fair fight. As Julián starts to walk away, El Jaibo hits him in the back of the head with the rock. He then beats Julián to death with a stick and takes his money. El Jaibo warns Pedro not to report the crime and shares Julián's money with Pedro to make him an [accomplice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accomplice "Accomplice").

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Los_olvidados_U.S._still_%281950%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Los_olvidados_U.S._still_%281950%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Los_olvidados_U.S._still_(1950)_(cropped).jpg)

[Alfonso Mejía](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Mej%C3%ADa "Alfonso Mejía") as Pedro (right, behind) in a publicity photo for the film

Pedro's mother resents her son's behavior, and shows that she doesn't love or care for him. Pedro is saddened by this, vows to start behaving better and finds work as apprentice to a blacksmith. One day, El Jaibo comes to talk with him about their secret and, unbeknownst to Pedro, steals a customer's knife from the blacksmith's table. Pedro is accused of the crime and sent to a juvenile rehabilitation program, the "farm school", where he gets into a fight and kills two chickens. The principal tests Pedro by handing Pedro a 50 [pesos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_peso "Mexican peso") bill to run errands with. Pedro accepts and leaves with the intention to complete the errands. As soon as he leaves, he encounters El Jaibo, who steals the money. Upset that his attempt to be good was foiled again, Pedro tracks down El Jaibo and fights him. The fight ends in a stalemate, but Pedro announces to the crowd that it was El Jaibo who killed Julián. El Jaibo flees, but the blind man has heard the accusation and tells the police.

Pedro tracks El Jaibo down once again to murder him. El Jaibo [kills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_murder "Child murder") Pedro. While fleeing, El Jaibo encounters the police and, as he tries to run away, the police shoot and kill him. Meche and her grandfather find Pedro's body in their shed. Not wanting to get involved, they dump his body down a garbage-covered cliff. On their way, they pass Pedro's mother, who, though once unconcerned with her disobedient child, is now searching for him.

## Alternate ending

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Alternate ending")]

In 2002, it was announced that an alternate ending for _Los Olvidados_ (labeled "the happy ending") was discovered at the Film Warehouse of the [National Autonomous University of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Autonomous_University_of_Mexico "National Autonomous University of Mexico"), and it would be restored digitally in order to show it to the public. On 8 July 2005, it was rescreened with the alternate ending in a few selected venues and included in subsequent DVD releases.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-5)

At the International Cinematographic Festival in Saltillo, Coahuila, Mexico, on 3 February 2011, the last surviving member of the cast, Alfonso Mejía (Pedro), introduced the alternative ending to the film.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-6)

The alternative ending begins with El Jaibo and Pedro fighting in an abandoned warehouse. Pedro pushes El Jaibo from the roof, where he falls to his death. Pedro frisks the body for the money El Jaibo stole from him (in contrast to the original ending, where Pedro is murdered by El Jaibo). Pedro returns to the farm school with the money that the principal entrusted to him.

## Analysis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Analysis")]

Thematically, _Los Olvidados_ is similar to Buñuel's earlier Spanish film, _[Land Without Bread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land\_Without\_Bread "Land Without Bread")_. Both films deal with the never-ending [cycle of poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_of_poverty "Cycle of poverty") and despair. _Los Olvidados_ is especially interesting because although "Buñuel employed [...] elements of [Italian neorealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_neorealism "Italian neorealism")", a concurrent movement across the Atlantic Ocean marked by "outdoor locations, nonprofessional actors, low budget productions, and a focus on the working classes", _Los Olvidados_ is not a neorealist film (Fernandez, 42). "Neorealist reality is incomplete, conventional, and above all rational", Buñuel wrote in a 1953 essay titled "Poetry and Cinema". "The poetry, the mystery, all that completes and enlarges tangible reality is utterly lacking" (Sklar, 324). _Los Olvidados_ contains such surrealistic shots as when "a boy throws an egg at the camera lens, where it shatters and drips" or a scene in which a boy has a dream in slow-motion (Sklar, 324). The surrealist dream sequence was actually shot in reverse and switched in post-production. Buñuel does not romanticize the characters, and even the abused blind man is revealed to have cruel habits of preying on children and selling fake elixirs. Film historian Carl J. Mora has said of Los olvidados that the director "visualized poverty in a radically different way from the traditional forms of Mexican melodrama. Buñuel's street children are not 'ennobled' by their desperate struggle for survival; they are in fact ruthless predators who are not better than their equally unromanticized victims".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-mora-9)

## Controversy about possible plagiarism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Controversy about possible plagiarism")]

Journalist Verónica Calderón, in an article published on 14 August 2010 in the Spanish newspaper [El País](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Pa%C3%ADs "El País"), collects statements by Morelia Guerrero, daughter of Mexican journalist and writer Jesús R. Guerrero ([Numarán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numar%C3%A1n "Numarán"), [Michoacán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michoac%C3%A1n "Michoacán"), 1911–1979), in which Morelia points out that the script and the film are based on a novel written by her father, entitled _Los Olvidados_, published in 1944, with a prologue by Mexican writer [José Revueltas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Revueltas "José Revueltas"). The [National Polytechnic Institute of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Polytechnic_Institute_of_Mexico "National Polytechnic Institute of Mexico") (IPN) published, in December 2009, a second edition of the novel penned by Jesús R. Guerrero.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-10) However, comparative studies have been made between the film and the novel, and no trace of any plagiarism by Buñuel has been found.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-11)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Initial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Initial")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Los_olvidados_U.S._still_%281950%29_2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Los_olvidados_U.S._still_%281950%29_2_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Los_olvidados_U.S._still_(1950)_2_(cropped).jpg)

Mario Ramírez and [Roberto Cobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Cobo "Roberto Cobo") (right) in a publicity still for the film

_Los Olvidados_ was largely disparaged by the Mexican press upon its release.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-12) Juan Carlos Ibáñez and Manuel Palacio write, "The film was so harsh and innovative, so critical and daring in its statements that during its first screenings, spectators openly aired their indignation towards the features of Mexican identity presented by Buñuel."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-13) The work was also criticized as overly bleak.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-14)

Critic for _The New Yorker,_ Pauline Kael wrote that in _Los Olvidados_ "Buñuel makes you understand the pornography of brutality: the pornography is in what human beings are capable of doing to other human beings."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-15)

### Retrospective

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Olvidados&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Retrospective")]

Many critics have since proclaimed _Los Olvidados_ a masterpiece. On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 91% of 43 critics' reviews are positive. The website's consensus reads: "_Los Olvidados_ casts an unsparing eye on juvenile crime -- and the systemically flawed societies that allow it to flourish."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-16) It was inscribed on [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s [Memory of the World International Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_of_the_World_International_Register "Memory of the World International Register") in 2003 in recognition of its historical significance.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-18)

The work placed 110th in the 2012 _[Sight & Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sight\_&\_Sound "Sight & Sound")_ critics' poll of the greatest films ever made.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-19) In April 2019, a restored version of the film was selected to be shown in the Cannes Classics section at the [2019 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Cannes_Film_Festival "2019 Cannes Film Festival").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-20) The film is ranked number 2 in the list of the best 100 Mexican films of all time according to 25 cinema critics (1994/2020).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Olvidados#cite_note-21)

**Louis Marie Malle** (French:[[lwi maʁi mal]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"); 30 October 1932 – 23 November 1995) was a French filmmaker who worked in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_France "Cinema of France") and [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States"). Described as "eclectic" and "difficult to pin down", his works often depict provocative or controversial subject matter.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-2)

Malle's most famous works include the crime thriller _[Elevator to the Gallows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator\_to\_the\_Gallows "Elevator to the Gallows")_ (1958), the romantic drama _[The Lovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lovers\_(1958\_film) "The Lovers (1958 film)")_ (1958), the World War II drama _[Lacombe, Lucien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacombe,\_Lucien "Lacombe, Lucien")_ (1974), the period drama _[Pretty Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty\_Baby\_(1978\_film) "Pretty Baby (1978 film)")_ (1978), the romantic crime film _[Atlantic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic\_City\_(1980\_film) "Atlantic City (1980 film)")_ (1980), the dramedy _[My Dinner with Andre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Dinner\_with\_Andre "My Dinner with Andre")_ (1981), and the autobiographical _[Au revoir les enfants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au\_revoir\_les\_enfants "Au revoir les enfants")_ (1987). He also co-directed the landmark underwater documentary _[The Silent World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silent\_World "The Silent World")_ with [Jacques Cousteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Cousteau "Jacques Cousteau"), which won the [1956](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Cannes_Film_Festival "1956 Cannes Film Festival")[Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or") and the [1957](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_Academy_Awards "29th Academy Awards")[Academy Award for Best Documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature_Film "Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature Film").

Critic [Pauline Kael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Kael "Pauline Kael") once wrote that the common quality of Malle's films was the "restless intelligence one senses in them".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-:0-3)

Malle is one of only four directors to have won the [Golden Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion") twice. His other accolades include three [César Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Awards "César Awards"), two [BAFTAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Awards "British Academy Film Awards"), and three [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") nominations. He was made a [Fellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Fellowship "BAFTA Fellowship") of the [British Academy of Film and Television Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") in [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/44th_British_Academy_Film_Awards#BAFTA_Fellowship "44th British Academy Film Awards").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-4)

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

### Early years and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years and education")]

Malle was born into a wealthy industrialist family in [Thumeries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thumeries "Thumeries"), [Nord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nord_(French_department) "Nord (French department)"), France, the son of Françoise (Béghin) and Pierre Malle.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-5) He was part Jewish, but raised as a Catholic.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-6)

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Malle attended a Catholic boarding school near Fontainebleau. As an 11-year-old he witnessed a [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo "Gestapo") raid on the school, in which three Jewish students, including his close friend, and a Jewish teacher were rounded up and deported to [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz_concentration_camp "Auschwitz concentration camp"). The school's headmaster, [Père Jacques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A8re_Jacques "Père Jacques"), was arrested for harboring them and sent to the concentration camp at [Mauthausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauthausen-Gusen_concentration_camp "Mauthausen-Gusen concentration camp"). Malle depicted these events in his autobiographical film _[Au revoir les enfants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au\_revoir\_les\_enfants "Au revoir les enfants")_ (1987).

As a young man, Malle studied political science at [Sciences Po](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciences_Po "Sciences Po") from 1950 to 1952 (some sources incorrectly state that he studied at the [Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris")) before turning to film studies at [IDHEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_des_hautes_%C3%A9tudes_cin%C3%A9matographiques "Institut des hautes études cinématographiques").

### Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

Malle worked as co-director and cameraman with [Jacques Cousteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques-Yves_Cousteau "Jacques-Yves Cousteau") on the documentary _[The Silent World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silent\_World "The Silent World")_ (1956), which won an [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature "Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature") and the [Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or") at the 1956 [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") and [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival"), respectively. He assisted [Robert Bresson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bresson "Robert Bresson") on _[A Man Escaped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Man\_Escaped "A Man Escaped")_ (_Un condamné à mort s'est échappé ou Le vent souffle où il veut_, 1956) before making his first feature, _[Ascenseur pour l'échafaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator\_to\_the\_Gallows "Elevator to the Gallows")_ in 1957 (released in the U.K. as _Lift to the Scaffold_ and in the U.S. originally as _Frantic_, later as _Elevator to the Gallows_). A taut thriller featuring an original score by [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), _Ascenseur pour l'échafaud_ made an international film star of [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau"), at the time a leading stage actress of the [Comédie-Française](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Com%C3%A9die-Fran%C3%A7aise "Comédie-Française"). Malle was 24 years old.

Malle's _[The Lovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lovers\_(1958\_film) "The Lovers (1958 film)")_ (_Les Amants_, 1958), which also starred Moreau, caused major controversy due to its sexual content, leading to a landmark [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case about the legal definition of obscenity. In _[Jacobellis v. Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobellis\_v.\_Ohio "Jacobellis v. Ohio")_, a theater owner was fined $2,500 for obscenity. The Supreme Court overturned the decision, finding that the film was not obscene and hence constitutionally protected. But the court could not agree on a definition of "obscene", with Justice [Potter Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potter_Stewart "Potter Stewart") famously saying, "[I know it when I see it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_know_it_when_I_see_it "I know it when I see it")".

Malle is sometimes associated with the _[nouvelle vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouvelle\_vague "Nouvelle vague")_, but his work does not directly fit in with or correspond to the auteurist theories that apply to the work of [Jean-Luc Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Godard "Jean-Luc Godard"), [François Truffaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Truffaut "François Truffaut"), [Claude Chabrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Chabrol "Claude Chabrol"), [Éric Rohmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ric_Rohmer "Éric Rohmer"), and others, and he had nothing to do with _[Cahiers du cinéma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahiers\_du\_cin%C3%A9ma "Cahiers du cinéma")_. But Malle's work does exemplify some of the movement's characteristics, such as using natural light and shooting on location, and his film _[Zazie dans le Métro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zazie\_dans\_le\_M%C3%A9tro "Zazie dans le Métro")_ (_Zazie in the Metro_, 1960, an adaptation of [the Raymond Queneau novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zazie_dans_le_M%C3%A9tro_(novel) "Zazie dans le Métro (novel)")) inspired Truffaut to write Malle an enthusiastic letter.

Other films also tackled taboo subjects: _[The Fire Within](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fire\_Within "The Fire Within")_ (also called _[Le Feu Follet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Feu\_Follet "Le Feu Follet")_) centers on a man about to commit suicide. Critic Pauline Kael said it should have solidified Malle's reputation in the U.S. as a great film director but suggested that its commercial failure may have been due to distribution issues.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-:0-3)_[Le souffle au cœur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_souffle\_au\_c%C5%93ur "Le souffle au cœur")_ (1971) deals with an incestuous relationship between mother and son, and _[Lacombe, Lucien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacombe,\_Lucien "Lacombe, Lucien")_ (1974), co-written with [Patrick Modiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Modiano "Patrick Modiano"), is about collaboration with the [Nazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi "Nazi") in [Vichy France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France") during World War II. The latter earned Malle his first Oscar nomination, for "Best Writing, Story and Screenplay Based on Factual Material or Material Not Previously Published or Produced".

### Documentary on India

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Documentary on India")]

Malle visited India in 1968, and made the seven-part documentary series _[L'Inde fantôme: Reflexions sur un voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom\_India "Phantom India")_ and the documentary film _[Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcutta\_(1969\_film) "Calcutta (1969 film)")_, which was released in cinemas.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-7) Concentrating on real India, its rituals and festivities, Malle fell afoul of the Indian government, which disliked his portrayal of the country, in its fascination with the pre-modern, and consequently banned the BBC from filming in India for several years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-malleind02-8) Malle later said his documentary on India was his favorite film.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-malleind02-8)

_Calcutta_ never opened in New York.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-:0-3)

### Move to the U.S.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Move to the U.S.")]

Malle later moved to the United States and continued to direct there. His later films include _[Pretty Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty\_Baby\_(1978\_film) "Pretty Baby (1978 film)")_ (1978), _[Atlantic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic\_City\_(1980\_film) "Atlantic City (1980 film)")_ (1980), _[My Dinner with Andre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Dinner\_with\_Andre "My Dinner with Andre")_ (1981), _[Crackers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crackers\_(1984\_film) "Crackers (1984 film)")_ (1984), _[Alamo Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamo\_Bay "Alamo Bay")_ (1985), _[Damage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damage\_(1992\_film) "Damage (1992 film)")_ (1992) and _[Vanya on 42nd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanya\_on\_42nd\_Street "Vanya on 42nd Street")_ (1994, an adaptation of [Anton Chekhov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Chekhov "Anton Chekhov")'s play _[Uncle Vanya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Vanya "Uncle Vanya")_) in English; and _[Au revoir les enfants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au\_revoir\_les\_enfants "Au revoir les enfants")_ (1987) and _[Milou en Mai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milou\_en\_Mai "Milou en Mai")_ (_May Fools_ in the U.S., 1990) in French. Just as his earlier films such as _The Lovers_ helped popularize French films in the U.S., _My Dinner with Andre_ was at the forefront of the rise of American independent cinema in the 1980s.

Towards the end of his life, cultural correspondent [Melinda Camber Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melinda_Camber_Porter "Melinda Camber Porter") interviewed Malle extensively for _The Times_. In 1993, the interviews were included in her book _Through Parisian Eyes: Reflections On Contemporary French Arts And Culture_.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Malle was married to actress [Anne-Marie Deschodt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne-Marie_Deschodt "Anne-Marie Deschodt") from 1965 to 1967. He later had a son, Manuel Cuotemoc Malle (born 1971), with German actress [Gila von Weitershausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gila_von_Weitershausen "Gila von Weitershausen"), and a daughter, filmmaker Justine Malle (born 1974), with Canadian actress [Alexandra Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Stewart "Alexandra Stewart").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-9) From mid-1977 until early 1980, he was in a relationship with [Susan Sarandon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Sarandon "Susan Sarandon").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-10)

Malle married actress [Candice Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candice_Bergen "Candice Bergen") in 1980. They had one child, [Chloé Françoise Malle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloe_Fran%C3%A7oise_Malle "Chloe Françoise Malle"), on 8 November 1985.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-11) Malle died of [lymphoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lymphoma "Lymphoma"), aged 63, at their home in Beverly Hills, California, on 23 November 1995.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-12)

**Louis Marie Malle** (French:[[lwi maʁi mal]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"); 30 October 1932 – 23 November 1995) was a French filmmaker who worked in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_France "Cinema of France") and [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States"). Described as "eclectic" and "difficult to pin down", his works often depict provocative or controversial subject matter.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-2)

Malle's most famous works include the crime thriller _[Elevator to the Gallows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator\_to\_the\_Gallows "Elevator to the Gallows")_ (1958), the romantic drama _[The Lovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lovers\_(1958\_film) "The Lovers (1958 film)")_ (1958), the World War II drama _[Lacombe, Lucien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacombe,\_Lucien "Lacombe, Lucien")_ (1974), the period drama _[Pretty Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty\_Baby\_(1978\_film) "Pretty Baby (1978 film)")_ (1978), the romantic crime film _[Atlantic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic\_City\_(1980\_film) "Atlantic City (1980 film)")_ (1980), the dramedy _[My Dinner with Andre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Dinner\_with\_Andre "My Dinner with Andre")_ (1981), and the autobiographical _[Au revoir les enfants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au\_revoir\_les\_enfants "Au revoir les enfants")_ (1987). He also co-directed the landmark underwater documentary _[The Silent World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silent\_World "The Silent World")_ with [Jacques Cousteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Cousteau "Jacques Cousteau"), which won the [1956](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Cannes_Film_Festival "1956 Cannes Film Festival")[Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or") and the [1957](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_Academy_Awards "29th Academy Awards")[Academy Award for Best Documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature_Film "Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature Film").

Critic [Pauline Kael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Kael "Pauline Kael") once wrote that the common quality of Malle's films was the "restless intelligence one senses in them".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-:0-3)

Malle is one of only four directors to have won the [Golden Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion") twice. His other accolades include three [César Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Awards "César Awards"), two [BAFTAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Awards "British Academy Film Awards"), and three [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") nominations. He was made a [Fellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Fellowship "BAFTA Fellowship") of the [British Academy of Film and Television Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") in [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/44th_British_Academy_Film_Awards#BAFTA_Fellowship "44th British Academy Film Awards").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-4)

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

### Early years and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years and education")]

Malle was born into a wealthy industrialist family in [Thumeries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thumeries "Thumeries"), [Nord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nord_(French_department) "Nord (French department)"), France, the son of Françoise (Béghin) and Pierre Malle.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-5) He was part Jewish, but raised as a Catholic.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-6)

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Malle attended a Catholic boarding school near Fontainebleau. As an 11-year-old he witnessed a [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo "Gestapo") raid on the school, in which three Jewish students, including his close friend, and a Jewish teacher were rounded up and deported to [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz_concentration_camp "Auschwitz concentration camp"). The school's headmaster, [Père Jacques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A8re_Jacques "Père Jacques"), was arrested for harboring them and sent to the concentration camp at [Mauthausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauthausen-Gusen_concentration_camp "Mauthausen-Gusen concentration camp"). Malle depicted these events in his autobiographical film _[Au revoir les enfants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au\_revoir\_les\_enfants "Au revoir les enfants")_ (1987).

As a young man, Malle studied political science at [Sciences Po](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciences_Po "Sciences Po") from 1950 to 1952 (some sources incorrectly state that he studied at the [Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris")) before turning to film studies at [IDHEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_des_hautes_%C3%A9tudes_cin%C3%A9matographiques "Institut des hautes études cinématographiques").

### Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

Malle worked as co-director and cameraman with [Jacques Cousteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques-Yves_Cousteau "Jacques-Yves Cousteau") on the documentary _[The Silent World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silent\_World "The Silent World")_ (1956), which won an [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature "Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature") and the [Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or") at the 1956 [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") and [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival"), respectively. He assisted [Robert Bresson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bresson "Robert Bresson") on _[A Man Escaped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Man\_Escaped "A Man Escaped")_ (_Un condamné à mort s'est échappé ou Le vent souffle où il veut_, 1956) before making his first feature, _[Ascenseur pour l'échafaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator\_to\_the\_Gallows "Elevator to the Gallows")_ in 1957 (released in the U.K. as _Lift to the Scaffold_ and in the U.S. originally as _Frantic_, later as _Elevator to the Gallows_). A taut thriller featuring an original score by [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), _Ascenseur pour l'échafaud_ made an international film star of [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau"), at the time a leading stage actress of the [Comédie-Française](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Com%C3%A9die-Fran%C3%A7aise "Comédie-Française"). Malle was 24 years old.

Malle's _[The Lovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lovers\_(1958\_film) "The Lovers (1958 film)")_ (_Les Amants_, 1958), which also starred Moreau, caused major controversy due to its sexual content, leading to a landmark [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case about the legal definition of obscenity. In _[Jacobellis v. Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobellis\_v.\_Ohio "Jacobellis v. Ohio")_, a theater owner was fined $2,500 for obscenity. The Supreme Court overturned the decision, finding that the film was not obscene and hence constitutionally protected. But the court could not agree on a definition of "obscene", with Justice [Potter Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potter_Stewart "Potter Stewart") famously saying, "[I know it when I see it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_know_it_when_I_see_it "I know it when I see it")".

Malle is sometimes associated with the _[nouvelle vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouvelle\_vague "Nouvelle vague")_, but his work does not directly fit in with or correspond to the auteurist theories that apply to the work of [Jean-Luc Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Godard "Jean-Luc Godard"), [François Truffaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Truffaut "François Truffaut"), [Claude Chabrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Chabrol "Claude Chabrol"), [Éric Rohmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ric_Rohmer "Éric Rohmer"), and others, and he had nothing to do with _[Cahiers du cinéma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahiers\_du\_cin%C3%A9ma "Cahiers du cinéma")_. But Malle's work does exemplify some of the movement's characteristics, such as using natural light and shooting on location, and his film _[Zazie dans le Métro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zazie\_dans\_le\_M%C3%A9tro "Zazie dans le Métro")_ (_Zazie in the Metro_, 1960, an adaptation of [the Raymond Queneau novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zazie_dans_le_M%C3%A9tro_(novel) "Zazie dans le Métro (novel)")) inspired Truffaut to write Malle an enthusiastic letter.

Other films also tackled taboo subjects: _[The Fire Within](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fire\_Within "The Fire Within")_ (also called _[Le Feu Follet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Feu\_Follet "Le Feu Follet")_) centers on a man about to commit suicide. Critic Pauline Kael said it should have solidified Malle's reputation in the U.S. as a great film director but suggested that its commercial failure may have been due to distribution issues.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-:0-3)_[Le souffle au cœur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_souffle\_au\_c%C5%93ur "Le souffle au cœur")_ (1971) deals with an incestuous relationship between mother and son, and _[Lacombe, Lucien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacombe,\_Lucien "Lacombe, Lucien")_ (1974), co-written with [Patrick Modiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Modiano "Patrick Modiano"), is about collaboration with the [Nazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi "Nazi") in [Vichy France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France") during World War II. The latter earned Malle his first Oscar nomination, for "Best Writing, Story and Screenplay Based on Factual Material or Material Not Previously Published or Produced".

### Documentary on India

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Documentary on India")]

Malle visited India in 1968, and made the seven-part documentary series _[L'Inde fantôme: Reflexions sur un voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom\_India "Phantom India")_ and the documentary film _[Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcutta\_(1969\_film) "Calcutta (1969 film)")_, which was released in cinemas.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-7) Concentrating on real India, its rituals and festivities, Malle fell afoul of the Indian government, which disliked his portrayal of the country, in its fascination with the pre-modern, and consequently banned the BBC from filming in India for several years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-malleind02-8) Malle later said his documentary on India was his favorite film.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-malleind02-8)

_Calcutta_ never opened in New York.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-:0-3)

### Move to the U.S.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Move to the U.S.")]

Malle later moved to the United States and continued to direct there. His later films include _[Pretty Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty\_Baby\_(1978\_film) "Pretty Baby (1978 film)")_ (1978), _[Atlantic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic\_City\_(1980\_film) "Atlantic City (1980 film)")_ (1980), _[My Dinner with Andre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Dinner\_with\_Andre "My Dinner with Andre")_ (1981), _[Crackers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crackers\_(1984\_film) "Crackers (1984 film)")_ (1984), _[Alamo Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamo\_Bay "Alamo Bay")_ (1985), _[Damage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damage\_(1992\_film) "Damage (1992 film)")_ (1992) and _[Vanya on 42nd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanya\_on\_42nd\_Street "Vanya on 42nd Street")_ (1994, an adaptation of [Anton Chekhov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Chekhov "Anton Chekhov")'s play _[Uncle Vanya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Vanya "Uncle Vanya")_) in English; and _[Au revoir les enfants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au\_revoir\_les\_enfants "Au revoir les enfants")_ (1987) and _[Milou en Mai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milou\_en\_Mai "Milou en Mai")_ (_May Fools_ in the U.S., 1990) in French. Just as his earlier films such as _The Lovers_ helped popularize French films in the U.S., _My Dinner with Andre_ was at the forefront of the rise of American independent cinema in the 1980s.

Towards the end of his life, cultural correspondent [Melinda Camber Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melinda_Camber_Porter "Melinda Camber Porter") interviewed Malle extensively for _The Times_. In 1993, the interviews were included in her book _Through Parisian Eyes: Reflections On Contemporary French Arts And Culture_.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Malle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Malle was married to actress [Anne-Marie Deschodt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne-Marie_Deschodt "Anne-Marie Deschodt") from 1965 to 1967. He later had a son, Manuel Cuotemoc Malle (born 1971), with German actress [Gila von Weitershausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gila_von_Weitershausen "Gila von Weitershausen"), and a daughter, filmmaker Justine Malle (born 1974), with Canadian actress [Alexandra Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Stewart "Alexandra Stewart").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-9) From mid-1977 until early 1980, he was in a relationship with [Susan Sarandon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Sarandon "Susan Sarandon").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-10)

Malle married actress [Candice Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candice_Bergen "Candice Bergen") in 1980. They had one child, [Chloé Françoise Malle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloe_Fran%C3%A7oise_Malle "Chloe Françoise Malle"), on 8 November 1985.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-11) Malle died of [lymphoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lymphoma "Lymphoma"), aged 63, at their home in Beverly Hills, California, on 23 November 1995.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle#cite_note-12)

_**The Criminal Life of Archibaldo de la Cruz**_ ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _**Ensayo de un crimen**_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'Rehearsal for a Crime'[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz#cite_note-1)) is a 1955 [Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Mexico "Cinema of Mexico")[crime comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_comedy "Crime comedy") film directed and co-written by Luis Buñuel and starring [Miroslava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslava_(actress) "Miroslava (actress)"), [Ernesto Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernesto_Alonso "Ernesto Alonso"), [Rita Macedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Macedo "Rita Macedo"), [Ariadna Welter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariadna_Welter "Ariadna Welter"), [Andrea Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Palma_(actress) "Andrea Palma (actress)") and [Leonor Llausás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonor_Llaus%C3%A1s "Leonor Llausás"). This film features the film debut of the actress Ariadna Welter and also the last appearance of Miroslava, in her film role, two months after her death in the same year. It is based on a 1944 novel by [Rodolfo Usigli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodolfo_Usigli "Rodolfo Usigli").

It tells the story of a would-be [serial killer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_killer "Serial killer") whose female victims keep dying before he has the chance to murder them.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Wealthy man Archibaldo de la Cruz tells a story about his childhood to a [nun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nun "Nun"). During the [Mexican Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Revolution "Mexican Revolution"), Archibaldo's indulgent mother gave him her special [music box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_box "Music box"), which his stern [governess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governess "Governess") said had the power to cause the death of one's enemies. To test the magic, Archibaldo wound up the box, and his governess was almost immediately struck by a stray bullet, leaving Archibaldo convinced that he killed her. Admitting he liked how powerful this made him feel, Archibaldo threatens the nun with a [straight razor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_razor "Straight razor"), but she runs away, only to fall down an open elevator shaft. When Archibaldo is called in by a judge investigating the incident, he confesses that he killed the nun, and she is not his first victim. Archibaldo then tells the judge a story:

A few weeks earlier, Archibaldo hears his music box playing in an antique shop. An attractive woman named Lavinia and her elderly fiancé are looking at it, but Archibaldo convinces the salesman to sell it to him instead by saying it belonged to his mother and was stolen during the Revolution. Back at home, Archibaldo plays the box and cuts himself shaving, the blood bringing back images of his governess' dead body.

Outside the home of Carlota Cervantes, a young woman he is courting, Archibaldo runs into Patricia Terrazas, who recognizes him from a gambling parlor they both used to frequent. Carlota's mother sees Archibaldo and warns Carlotta, who is with her married lover, the architect Alejandro Rivas. Archibaldo gives Carlota a vase he made and says he has feelings that scare him, but believes he can be saved by her purity. A jealous Alejandro wants to interrupt, so, to avoid a scene, Carlota's mother says Carlota has to leave.

At the gambling parlor, Archibaldo sees Patricia. He hears her argue with her lover, Willy Corduran, and follows when she storms off. She crashes Willy's car, and Archibaldo offers to drive her home, stopping at his house to get his razor. While Patricia pours them drinks, Archibaldo imagines killing her and prepares to do it for real, but Willy enters, interrupting his plan. Patricia admits she was just trying to make Willy jealous, and Archibaldo leaves when the couple begin to kiss, though they are already arguing by the time he walks out the door. In the morning, a police detective tells Archibaldo that Patricia has committed suicide.

Carlota avoids a phone call from Archibaldo, so he goes to a bar alone. He sees Lavinia and is transfixed, as she appears to be surrounded by the [flames from her drink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flaming_drink "Flaming drink"). Lavinia comes over, mostly to get a break from the American tourists she is showing around. Her fiancé arrives, and she gives Archibaldo an address where she can be contacted, before excusing herself.

Archibaldo visits Carlota and proposes, but she says she needs a month or two to decide. He goes to the address Lavinia gave him and discovers it is a dress shop. No one has heard of Lavinia, but there is a [mannequin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannequin "Mannequin") that looks just like her. Remembering that, as well as a [tour guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_guide "Tour guide"), she mentioned working as a model for artists, he asks who made the mannequin and visits the artist's studio. Lavinia is there and is impressed he found her. After being reassured he does not live alone, she agrees to come to his home, supposedly to model.

Carlota visits Alejandro at work to tell him they have to break up, even though she still loves him, since his wife refuses to grant a divorce. He guesses that Archibaldo proposed and says he will not let Carlota go so easily.

The day Lavinia is to visit, Archibaldo sends his servants away. He introduces her to the cousin he said lives with him, and she is amused to discover the "cousin" is really the mannequin, which he purchased. While he is out of the room firing up his [kiln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiln "Kiln") and getting drinks, Lavinia swaps clothes with the mannequin to play a trick on Archibaldo. He tries to kiss her, but she resists, so he kisses the mannequin, and then Lavinia kisses him. She begins to remove her clothes from the mannequin, but Archibaldo asks her to leave them and keep the mannequin's more-expensive clothes.

Archibaldo has Lavinia look at a childhood photo album and is sneaking up behind her when the doorbell rings. He answers it, and a group of tourists burst in. Lavinia innocently claims she invited them to tour his pottery studio, but he is angered by her trick. She says she is getting married, so she is quitting her job and will not see him again.

After Lavinia leaves with the tourists, Archibaldo takes the mannequin and puts it in his kiln, watching with a perverse glee as it melts. Carlota and her mother arrive to say Carlota has accepted the proposal, which overjoys Archibaldo, though Carlota seems ambivalent, and her mother bursts into tears.

Shortly before the wedding, Archibaldo gets a letter telling him to go to Alejandro's apartment. He watches from outside as Carlota enters and Alejandro closes the blinds. She asks Alejandro not to interfere in her wedding, to which he agrees, but he also says he feels something will keep them from being parted. Disappointed that Carlota does not seem to be as pure as he thought, Archibaldo fantasizes about shooting her on their wedding night in her wedding gown after making her pray, but this plan is foiled when, just after the ceremony, Alejandro shoots her instead.

Having heard Archibaldo's confession, the judge says that, while Archibaldo has the potential to be a criminal, he has committed no crimes. Still feeling responsible for the women's deaths, Archibaldo returns home and listens to the music box. Suddenly, he stops it, goes to a park, and throws it in a lake. Immediately, he feels better. He runs into Lavinia, and learns she did not get married after all. They link arms and walk away together.

## Academic criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Academic criticism")]

_Ensayo de un crimen_ has been analyzed and studied by academics and critics such as Victor Fuentes, Gerardo T. Cummings, Marsha Kinder, and Ilan Stavans. Fuentes, a retired professor from the [University of California, Santa Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Barbara "University of California, Santa Barbara"), included chapters dedicated to the detailed analytical study of the film in his book, _La mirada de Buñuel_ (Spain: Tabla Rasa Libros y Ediciones, 2006), finding correlations between _Ensayo de un crimen_ and _Él_. In 2004, Cummings published an article in the Puerto Rican journal _Revista Horizontes_, in which he analyzed the intertextual connections between the film and its literary source, the novel of the same name by [Rodolfo Usigli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodolfo_Usigli "Rodolfo Usigli") (this article was part of a larger dissertation chapter on the echoes of the novel in the film).

The film's exploration of obsessive desire has been compared to [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock")'s [_Vertigo_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo_(film) "Vertigo (film)") (1958).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz#cite_note-3)

In 2002, _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant\_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_ called the film "a twisted [tragicomedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragicomedy "Tragicomedy") on male obsession [...] the closest Spanish [auteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auteur "Auteur") Luis Buñuel ever came to directing a bona fide [suspense thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspense_thriller "Suspense thriller")."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz#cite_note-4)

Buñuel briefly references the production of _Ensayo de un crimen_ in his 1983 autobiography _Mon dernier soupir_ (_My Last Breath_). In it, he recounts how he was syndicated into orchestrating an original composition for the movie, and that, when the members of the orchestra disrobed due to heat, he saw that "at least 3/4ths of them carried holstered guns". Later in the book, Buñuel sadly recalls the ironic parallel between a scene where the protagonist cremates a wax mannequin based on Miroslava, and Miroslava's actual cremation following her suicide shortly after production wrapped.

_**The Criminal Life of Archibaldo de la Cruz**_ ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _**Ensayo de un crimen**_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'Rehearsal for a Crime'[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz#cite_note-1)) is a 1955 [Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Mexico "Cinema of Mexico")[crime comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_comedy "Crime comedy") film directed and co-written by Luis Buñuel and starring [Miroslava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslava_(actress) "Miroslava (actress)"), [Ernesto Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernesto_Alonso "Ernesto Alonso"), [Rita Macedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Macedo "Rita Macedo"), [Ariadna Welter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariadna_Welter "Ariadna Welter"), [Andrea Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Palma_(actress) "Andrea Palma (actress)") and [Leonor Llausás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonor_Llaus%C3%A1s "Leonor Llausás"). This film features the film debut of the actress Ariadna Welter and also the last appearance of Miroslava, in her film role, two months after her death in the same year. It is based on a 1944 novel by [Rodolfo Usigli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodolfo_Usigli "Rodolfo Usigli").

It tells the story of a would-be [serial killer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_killer "Serial killer") whose female victims keep dying before he has the chance to murder them.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Wealthy man Archibaldo de la Cruz tells a story about his childhood to a [nun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nun "Nun"). During the [Mexican Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Revolution "Mexican Revolution"), Archibaldo's indulgent mother gave him her special [music box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_box "Music box"), which his stern [governess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governess "Governess") said had the power to cause the death of one's enemies. To test the magic, Archibaldo wound up the box, and his governess was almost immediately struck by a stray bullet, leaving Archibaldo convinced that he killed her. Admitting he liked how powerful this made him feel, Archibaldo threatens the nun with a [straight razor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_razor "Straight razor"), but she runs away, only to fall down an open elevator shaft. When Archibaldo is called in by a judge investigating the incident, he confesses that he killed the nun, and she is not his first victim. Archibaldo then tells the judge a story:

A few weeks earlier, Archibaldo hears his music box playing in an antique shop. An attractive woman named Lavinia and her elderly fiancé are looking at it, but Archibaldo convinces the salesman to sell it to him instead by saying it belonged to his mother and was stolen during the Revolution. Back at home, Archibaldo plays the box and cuts himself shaving, the blood bringing back images of his governess' dead body.

Outside the home of Carlota Cervantes, a young woman he is courting, Archibaldo runs into Patricia Terrazas, who recognizes him from a gambling parlor they both used to frequent. Carlota's mother sees Archibaldo and warns Carlotta, who is with her married lover, the architect Alejandro Rivas. Archibaldo gives Carlota a vase he made and says he has feelings that scare him, but believes he can be saved by her purity. A jealous Alejandro wants to interrupt, so, to avoid a scene, Carlota's mother says Carlota has to leave.

At the gambling parlor, Archibaldo sees Patricia. He hears her argue with her lover, Willy Corduran, and follows when she storms off. She crashes Willy's car, and Archibaldo offers to drive her home, stopping at his house to get his razor. While Patricia pours them drinks, Archibaldo imagines killing her and prepares to do it for real, but Willy enters, interrupting his plan. Patricia admits she was just trying to make Willy jealous, and Archibaldo leaves when the couple begin to kiss, though they are already arguing by the time he walks out the door. In the morning, a police detective tells Archibaldo that Patricia has committed suicide.

Carlota avoids a phone call from Archibaldo, so he goes to a bar alone. He sees Lavinia and is transfixed, as she appears to be surrounded by the [flames from her drink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flaming_drink "Flaming drink"). Lavinia comes over, mostly to get a break from the American tourists she is showing around. Her fiancé arrives, and she gives Archibaldo an address where she can be contacted, before excusing herself.

Archibaldo visits Carlota and proposes, but she says she needs a month or two to decide. He goes to the address Lavinia gave him and discovers it is a dress shop. No one has heard of Lavinia, but there is a [mannequin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannequin "Mannequin") that looks just like her. Remembering that, as well as a [tour guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_guide "Tour guide"), she mentioned working as a model for artists, he asks who made the mannequin and visits the artist's studio. Lavinia is there and is impressed he found her. After being reassured he does not live alone, she agrees to come to his home, supposedly to model.

Carlota visits Alejandro at work to tell him they have to break up, even though she still loves him, since his wife refuses to grant a divorce. He guesses that Archibaldo proposed and says he will not let Carlota go so easily.

The day Lavinia is to visit, Archibaldo sends his servants away. He introduces her to the cousin he said lives with him, and she is amused to discover the "cousin" is really the mannequin, which he purchased. While he is out of the room firing up his [kiln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiln "Kiln") and getting drinks, Lavinia swaps clothes with the mannequin to play a trick on Archibaldo. He tries to kiss her, but she resists, so he kisses the mannequin, and then Lavinia kisses him. She begins to remove her clothes from the mannequin, but Archibaldo asks her to leave them and keep the mannequin's more-expensive clothes.

Archibaldo has Lavinia look at a childhood photo album and is sneaking up behind her when the doorbell rings. He answers it, and a group of tourists burst in. Lavinia innocently claims she invited them to tour his pottery studio, but he is angered by her trick. She says she is getting married, so she is quitting her job and will not see him again.

After Lavinia leaves with the tourists, Archibaldo takes the mannequin and puts it in his kiln, watching with a perverse glee as it melts. Carlota and her mother arrive to say Carlota has accepted the proposal, which overjoys Archibaldo, though Carlota seems ambivalent, and her mother bursts into tears.

Shortly before the wedding, Archibaldo gets a letter telling him to go to Alejandro's apartment. He watches from outside as Carlota enters and Alejandro closes the blinds. She asks Alejandro not to interfere in her wedding, to which he agrees, but he also says he feels something will keep them from being parted. Disappointed that Carlota does not seem to be as pure as he thought, Archibaldo fantasizes about shooting her on their wedding night in her wedding gown after making her pray, but this plan is foiled when, just after the ceremony, Alejandro shoots her instead.

Having heard Archibaldo's confession, the judge says that, while Archibaldo has the potential to be a criminal, he has committed no crimes. Still feeling responsible for the women's deaths, Archibaldo returns home and listens to the music box. Suddenly, he stops it, goes to a park, and throws it in a lake. Immediately, he feels better. He runs into Lavinia, and learns she did not get married after all. They link arms and walk away together.

## Academic criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Academic criticism")]

_Ensayo de un crimen_ has been analyzed and studied by academics and critics such as Victor Fuentes, Gerardo T. Cummings, Marsha Kinder, and Ilan Stavans. Fuentes, a retired professor from the [University of California, Santa Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Barbara "University of California, Santa Barbara"), included chapters dedicated to the detailed analytical study of the film in his book, _La mirada de Buñuel_ (Spain: Tabla Rasa Libros y Ediciones, 2006), finding correlations between _Ensayo de un crimen_ and _Él_. In 2004, Cummings published an article in the Puerto Rican journal _Revista Horizontes_, in which he analyzed the intertextual connections between the film and its literary source, the novel of the same name by [Rodolfo Usigli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodolfo_Usigli "Rodolfo Usigli") (this article was part of a larger dissertation chapter on the echoes of the novel in the film).

The film's exploration of obsessive desire has been compared to [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock")'s [_Vertigo_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo_(film) "Vertigo (film)") (1958).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz#cite_note-3)

In 2002, _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant\_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_ called the film "a twisted [tragicomedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragicomedy "Tragicomedy") on male obsession [...] the closest Spanish [auteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auteur "Auteur") Luis Buñuel ever came to directing a bona fide [suspense thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspense_thriller "Suspense thriller")."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criminal_Life_of_Archibaldo_de_la_Cruz#cite_note-4)

Buñuel briefly references the production of _Ensayo de un crimen_ in his 1983 autobiography _Mon dernier soupir_ (_My Last Breath_). In it, he recounts how he was syndicated into orchestrating an original composition for the movie, and that, when the members of the orchestra disrobed due to heat, he saw that "at least 3/4ths of them carried holstered guns". Later in the book, Buñuel sadly recalls the ironic parallel between a scene where the protagonist cremates a wax mannequin based on Miroslava, and Miroslava's actual cremation following her suicide shortly after production wrapped.
