### 1957–1969: Directorial debut and early work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1957–1969: Directorial debut and early work")]

Altman's first forays into television directing were on the [DuMont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuMont_Television_Network "DuMont Television Network") drama series _[Pulse of the City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulse\_of\_the\_City "Pulse of the City")_ (1953–1954), and an episode of the 1956 western series _[The Sheriff of Cochise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sheriff\_of\_Cochise "The Sheriff of Cochise")_. In 1956 he was hired by a local businessman to write and direct a feature film in Kansas City on [juvenile delinquency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenile_delinquency "Juvenile delinquency"). The film, titled _[The Delinquents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Delinquents\_(1957\_film) "The Delinquents (1957 film)")_, made for $60,000, was purchased by [United Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists "United Artists") for $150,000, and released in 1957. While primitive, this teen [exploitation film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploitation_film "Exploitation film") contained the foundations of Altman's later work in its use of casual, naturalistic dialogue. With its success, Altman moved from Kansas City to California for the last time. He co-directed _[The James Dean Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_James\_Dean\_Story "The James Dean Story")_ (1957), a documentary rushed into theaters to capitalize on the actor's recent death and marketed to his emerging cult following. Both works caught the attention of [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock") who hired Altman as a director for his [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") anthology series _[Alfred Hitchcock Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred\_Hitchcock\_Presents "Alfred Hitchcock Presents")_. After just two episodes, Altman resigned due to differences with a producer, but this exposure enabled him to forge a successful television career. Over the next decade Altman worked prolifically in television (and almost exclusively in series dramas) directing multiple episodes of _[Whirlybirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whirlybirds "Whirlybirds")_, _[The Millionaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Millionaire\_(TV\_series) "The Millionaire (TV series)")_, _[U.S. Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S.\_Marshal\_(TV\_series) "U.S. Marshal (TV series)")_, _[The Troubleshooters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Troubleshooters\_(1959\_TV\_series) "The Troubleshooters (1959 TV series)")_, _[The Roaring 20s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Roaring\_20s\_(TV\_series) "The Roaring 20s (TV series)")_, _[Bonanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonanza "Bonanza")_, _[Bus Stop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus\_Stop\_(TV\_series) "Bus Stop (TV series)")_, _[Kraft Mystery Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kraft\_Mystery\_Theater "Kraft Mystery Theater")_, _[Combat!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat! "Combat!")_, as well as single episodes of several other notable series including _[Hawaiian Eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian\_Eye "Hawaiian Eye")_, _[Maverick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maverick\_(TV\_series) "Maverick (TV series)")_ (the fourth season episode ["Bolt From the Blue"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maverick_episodes "List of Maverick episodes") also written by Altman and starring [Roger Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Moore "Roger Moore")), _[Lawman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawman\_(TV\_series) "Lawman (TV series)")_, _[Surfside 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surfside\_6 "Surfside 6")_, _[Peter Gunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter\_Gunn "Peter Gunn")_, and _[Route 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route\_66\_(TV\_series) "Route 66 (TV series)")_.

By the 1960s Altman had established himself as a television director due to his ability to work quickly and efficiently on a limited budget. Though he was frequently fired from television projects for refusing to conform to network mandates, Altman always was able to land new assignments. In 1964 the producers decided to expand "Once Upon a Savage Night", one of his episodes of _[Kraft Suspense Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kraft\_Suspense\_Theatre "Kraft Suspense Theatre")_, for release as a television film under the title _[Nightmare in Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightmare\_in\_Chicago "Nightmare in Chicago")_. In a 1963 episode, "The Hunt", his cast included [James Caan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Caan "James Caan") and [Bruce Dern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Dern "Bruce Dern").

Two years later Altman was hired to direct the low-budget space travel feature _[Countdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown\_(1967\_film) "Countdown (1967 film)")_, but was fired within days of the project's conclusion because he had refused to edit the film to a manageable length. He worked with Caan again, who led the cast with [Robert Duvall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Duvall "Robert Duvall"). He did not direct another film until _[That Cold Day in the Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That\_Cold\_Day\_in\_the\_Park "That Cold Day in the Park")_ (1969), which was a critical and box-office disaster. During the decade, Altman began to express political subtexts within his works. In particular he expressed anti-war sentiments regarding the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). Because of this, Altman's career would somewhat suffer as he came to be associated with the [anti-war movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_to_United_States_involvement_in_the_Vietnam_War "Opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War").

### 1970–1979: Breakthrough and stardom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1970–1979: Breakthrough and stardom")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Shelley_Duvall_1975.jpg/250px-Shelley_Duvall_1975.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shelley_Duvall_1975.jpg)

[Shelley Duvall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelley_Duvall "Shelley Duvall") was a muse of Altman's, acting in seven of his films including _[Brewster McCloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster\_McCloud "Brewster McCloud")_ (1970), _[Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_(film) "Nashville (film)")_ (1975), _[3 Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3\_Women "3 Women")_ (1977), and _[Popeye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popeye\_(1980\_film) "Popeye (1980 film)")_ (1980)

In 1969 Altman was offered the script for _[M*A*S*H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MASH\_(film) "MASH (film)")_, an adaptation of a little-known [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War")-era novel satirizing life in the armed services; more than a dozen other filmmakers had passed on it. Altman had been hesitant to take the production, and the shoot was so tumultuous that [Elliott Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott_Gould "Elliott Gould") and [Donald Sutherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Sutherland "Donald Sutherland") tried to have Altman fired over his unorthodox filming methods. Nevertheless, _M*A*S*H_ was widely hailed as a classic upon its 1970 release. It won the _[Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme\_d'Or "Palme d'Or")_ at the 1970 [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") and netted five [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award "Academy Award") nominations. It was Altman's highest-grossing film, released during a time of increasing anti-war sentiment in the United States. The [Academy Film Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Film_Archive "Academy Film Archive") preserved _M*A*S*H_ in 2000.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-13)

Now recognized as a major talent, Altman notched critical successes with _[McCabe & Mrs. Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCabe\_&\_Mrs.\_Miller "McCabe & Mrs. Miller")_ (1971), a [revisionist Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revisionist_Western "Revisionist Western") in which the mordant songs of [Leonard Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Cohen "Leonard Cohen") underscore a gritty vision of the American frontier; _[Images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Images\_(film) "Images (film)")_, his single, [Bergman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingmar_Bergman "Ingmar Bergman")-inspired attempt at making a horror film; _[The Long Goodbye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Long\_Goodbye\_(film) "The Long Goodbye (film)")_ (1973), a controversial adaptation of the [Raymond Chandler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Chandler "Raymond Chandler") novel (scripted by [Leigh Brackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leigh_Brackett "Leigh Brackett")) now ranked as a seminal influence on the [neo-noir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-noir "Neo-noir") subgenre; _[Thieves Like Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thieves\_Like\_Us\_(film) "Thieves Like Us (film)")_ (1974), an adaptation of the Edward Anderson novel previously filmed by [Nicholas Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Ray "Nicholas Ray") as _[They Live by Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/They\_Live\_by\_Night "They Live by Night")_ (1949); _[California Split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California\_Split "California Split")_ (1974), a gambling comedy-drama shot partially on location in [Reno, Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reno,_Nevada "Reno, Nevada"); and _[Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_(film) "Nashville (film)")_ (1975), which had a strong political theme set against the world of [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"). The stars of the film wrote their own songs; [Keith Carradine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Carradine "Keith Carradine") won an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") for the song "[I'm Easy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Easy_(Keith_Carradine_song) "I'm Easy (Keith Carradine song)")". Altman's next film, _[Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo\_Bill\_and\_the\_Indians,\_or\_Sitting\_Bull's\_History\_Lesson "Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson")_, won the [Golden Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Bear "Golden Bear") at the [28th Berlin International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/28th_Berlin_International_Film_Festival "28th Berlin International Film Festival").

Although his films were often met with divisive notices, and some, like _[A Perfect Couple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Perfect\_Couple\_(1979\_film) "A Perfect Couple (1979 film)")_ and _[Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintet\_(film) "Quintet (film)")_ were widely panned, many of the prominent film critics of the era (including [Pauline Kael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Kael "Pauline Kael"), [Vincent Canby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Canby "Vincent Canby") and [Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert")) remained steadfastly loyal to his directorial style throughout the decade. Audiences took some time to appreciate his films, and he did not want to have to satisfy studio officials. In 1970, following the release of _M*A*S*H,_ he founded Lion's Gate Films to have independent production freedom. Altman's company is not to be confused with the current [Lionsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lions_Gate_Entertainment "Lions Gate Entertainment"), a Canada/U.S. entertainment company.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-14) The films he made through his company included _[Brewster McCloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster\_McCloud "Brewster McCloud")_, _[A Wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Wedding\_(1978\_film) "A Wedding (1978 film)")_, and _[3 Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3\_Women "3 Women")_.

### 1980–1991: Career fluctuations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1980–1991: Career fluctuations")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Robert_Altman_-_1976.jpg/250px-Robert_Altman_-_1976.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Altman_-_1976.jpg)

Altman with [Lillian Gish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Gish "Lillian Gish") and [Lily Tomlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lily_Tomlin "Lily Tomlin") at _Nashville_ awards ceremony in 1976

In 1980, he directed the musical film _[Popeye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popeye\_(film) "Popeye (film)")_. Produced by [Robert Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Evans_(film_producer) "Robert Evans (film producer)") and written by [Jules Feiffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jules_Feiffer "Jules Feiffer"), the film was based on the comic strip / cartoon [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popeye "Popeye") and starred [Shelley Duvall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelley_Duvall "Shelley Duvall") and the comedian [Robin Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Williams "Robin Williams") in his film debut. [Gilda Radner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilda_Radner "Gilda Radner") was also considered for the lead female role;[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Bradford-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-16) her manager, [Bernie Brillstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Brillstein "Bernie Brillstein"), discouraged her from taking the role, in part due to his worries of her working for months on an isolated set with Altman, known for his erratic behavior and unorthodox creative methods.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-17) Designed as a vehicle to increase Altman's commercial clout following a series of critically acclaimed but commercially unsuccessful low-budget films in the late 1970s (including _3 Women_, _A Wedding_, and _Quintet_), _Popeye_ was filmed on location in [Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malta "Malta"). It was soon beleaguered by heavy drug and alcohol use among most of the cast and crew, including the director; Altman reportedly clashed with Evans, Williams (who threatened to leave the film), and songwriter [Harry Nilsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Nilsson "Harry Nilsson") (who departed midway through the shoot, leaving [Van Dyke Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Dyke_Parks "Van Dyke Parks") to finish the orchestrations). Although the film grossed $60 million worldwide on a $20 million budget and was the second highest-grossing film Altman had directed to that point, it failed to meet studio expectations and was considered a box office disappointment.

In 1981 the director sold Lion's Gate to producer [Jonathan Taplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Taplin "Jonathan Taplin") after his political satire _[Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health\_(film) "Health (film)")_ (shot in early 1979 for a Christmas release) was shelved by longtime distributor [20th Century Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Fox "20th Century Fox") following tepid test and festival screenings throughout 1980. The departure of longtime Altman partisan [Alan Ladd Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Ladd_Jr. "Alan Ladd Jr.") from Fox also played a decisive role in forestalling the release of the film.

Unable to secure major financing in the post-New Hollywood [blockbuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbuster_(entertainment) "Blockbuster (entertainment)") era because of his mercurial reputation and the particularly tumultuous events surrounding the production of _Popeye_, Altman returned to television and theater between films. His first project after _Popeye_ was _2 by South_, a double bill of plays by unknown playwright Frank South, _Rattlesnake in a Cooler_ and _Precious Blood_. The production debuted in Los Angeles and transferred off-Broadway, before Altman adapted it as a pair of television films. Altman's next project was to revive [Ed Graczyk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Graczyk "Ed Graczyk")'s play, [_Come Back to the 5 & Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come_Back_to_the_5_&_Dime,_Jimmy_Dean,_Jimmy_Dean_(play) "Come Back to the 5 & Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean (play)"). Like _2 by South_, Altman adapted his production as a film. [The film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come_Back_to_the_Five_and_Dime,_Jimmy_Dean,_Jimmy_Dean_(film) "Come Back to the Five and Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean (film)"), which starred [Cher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cher "Cher"), [Karen Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Black "Karen Black"), and [Sandy Dennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Dennis "Sandy Dennis"), played at film festivals before its independent theatrical release; Altman turned down several distribution deals to keep the film under his control.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-McGilligan-18):115

In 1982, after finishing work on _Come Back to the Five and Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean_, Altman travelled to Dallas to film his next film, [_Streamers_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streamers_(film) "Streamers (film)"). The film, adapted by [David Rabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Rabe "David Rabe") from his [hit play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streamers_(play) "Streamers (play)"), was shot in only 18 days. Its 1983 release made it Altman's third theatrical adaptation in as many years. Afterwards, he began teaching a course on his films at the [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan"), where he concurrently staged his first production of [Igor Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky")'s _[The Rake's Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Rake's\_Progress "The Rake's Progress")_. He also co-wrote [John Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Anderson_(musician) "John Anderson (musician)")'s 1983 hit single "[Black Sheep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sheep_(John_Anderson_song) "Black Sheep (John Anderson song)")".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-19)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Altman_01.jpg/250px-Altman_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Altman_01.jpg)

Altman in 1980

After the critical success of his three successive theatrical adaptations, Altman attempted to return to Hollywood with the [teen comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_comedy "Teen comedy")_[O.C. and Stiggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O.C.\_and\_Stiggs "O.C. and Stiggs")_ (1985). Like _Popeye_, the chaotic production was characterized by tension between Altman and the studio, [MGM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM "MGM"). Altman travelled to Arizona to shoot away from the executives and the screenwriters, whom he banned from the set. There he shot the film in the summer of 1983, but poor test screenings, chaos within the studio, and changing ownership delayed the film's release. It finally received a belated limited commercial release in 1987, four years after it was shot.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-20) The [British Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British Film Institute") later referred to it as "probably Altman's least successful film".

While _O.C. and Stiggs_ was shelved, Altman returned to theatrical adaptations and to the University of Michigan to film _[Secret Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret\_Honor "Secret Honor")_, using his students as crew members. Based on a one man-play about former president [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon"), the film starred [Philip Baker Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Baker_Hall "Philip Baker Hall") as the ex-president. In 2008, the University of Michigan Library acquired Altman's archive.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-ManyHatsUMich-21) Adapted by Altman and [Sam Shepard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Shepard "Sam Shepard") for [The Cannon Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cannon_Group "The Cannon Group") from Shepard's [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize")-nominated play, _[Fool for Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fool\_for\_Love\_(1985\_film) "Fool for Love (1985 film)")_ (1985) featured the playwright-actor alongside [Kim Basinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Basinger "Kim Basinger"), [Harry Dean Stanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Dean_Stanton "Harry Dean Stanton"), and [Randy Quaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Quaid "Randy Quaid"); it fared better than most of his films from the era, earning $900,000 domestically on a $2 million budget and positive reviews from [Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") and [Vincent Canby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Canby "Vincent Canby").

Disappointed by his string of critical and commercial failures, including the still-unreleased _O.C. and Stiggs_, Altman moved to Paris. There, he shot another television film, _[The Laundromat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Laundromat\_(1985\_film) "The Laundromat (1985 film)")_, which he completed before _Fool for Love_. He then wrote and directed _[Beyond Therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyond\_Therapy\_(film) "Beyond Therapy (film)")_, which proved to be one of his biggest failures. Altman then mounted his second production of _The Rake's Progress_, this time at the prestigious [Opéra de Lille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Op%C3%A9ra_de_Lille "Opéra de Lille"). The Opéra was undergoing financial collapse at the time, and its failure to regain money through ambitious productions caused it close later that year. Altman also used a selection from Jean-Phillipe Rameau's _[Les Boréades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les\_Bor%C3%A9ades "Les Boréades")_ as the basis for his contribution to _[Aria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria\_(1987\_film) "Aria (1987 film)")_, which was shown at the [1987 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Cannes_Film_Festival "1987 Cannes Film Festival") to mixed reception. Altman made his next television film, _Basements_, based on two plays by Harold Pinter. Though Pinter wrote the screenplay himself, this film became the latest of Altman's failures. The long-awaited release of _O.C. and Stiggs_ that year was also panned.

Altman finally regained a modicum of critical favor in 1988 for his television work. He returned to America early that year to shoot the [mockumentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mockumentary "Mockumentary") show _[Tanner '88](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanner\_'88 "Tanner '88")_ (1988), a collaboration with [Garry Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garry_Trudeau "Garry Trudeau") set in the milieu of a United States presidential campaign, for which he earned a [Primetime Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award "Primetime Emmy Award"). The series was shot on the actual campaign trail and featured several real candidates. During the show's run, Altman's television production of _[The Caine Mutiny Court-Martial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Caine\_Mutiny\_Court-Martial\_(1988\_film) "The Caine Mutiny Court-Martial (1988 film)")_ aired. Though it received high acclaim, it would be his last television film. In 1990, Altman directed _[Vincent & Theo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent\_&\_Theo "Vincent & Theo")_, a biographical film about [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh") that was intended as a television miniseries for broadcast in the United Kingdom. A theatrical version of the film was a modest success in the United States, marking a significant turning point in the director's critical resurgence.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-23)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-25)

### 1992–2006: Career resurgence and final films

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1992–2006: Career resurgence and final films")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Robert_Altman_Cannes.jpg/250px-Robert_Altman_Cannes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Altman_Cannes.jpg)

Altman at the 1992 Cannes Film Festival

He revitalized his career in earnest with _[The Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Player\_(1992\_film) "The Player (1992 film)")_ (1992), a satire of Hollywood. Co-produced by the influential [David Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Brown_(producer) "David Brown (producer)") (_[The Sting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sting "The Sting")_, _[Jaws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaws\_(film) "Jaws (film)")_, _[Cocoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocoon\_(film) "Cocoon (film)")_), the film was nominated for three Academy Awards, including [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director"). While he did not win the Oscar, he was awarded Best Director by the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival"), [BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA"), and the [New York Film Critics Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Film_Critics_Circle "New York Film Critics Circle").

Altman then directed _[Short Cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short\_Cuts\_(film) "Short Cuts (film)")_ (1993), an ambitious adaptation of several short stories by [Raymond Carver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Carver "Raymond Carver"), which portrayed the lives of various citizens of Los Angeles over the course of several days. The film's large cast and intertwining of many different storylines were similar to his large-cast films of the 1970s; he won the [Golden Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion") at the 1993 [Venice International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_International_Film_Festival "Venice International Film Festival") and another Oscar nomination for Best Director.

Between shooting and editing _[Short Cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short\_Cuts "Short Cuts")_, Altman made his return to opera as the director and co-librettist of [_McTeague_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McTeague_(opera) "McTeague (opera)"). Altman was hired on the project by [William Bolcom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bolcom "William Bolcom"), who had been commissioned with his regular librettist, [Arnold Weinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Weinstein "Arnold Weinstein"), to write an opera by the [Lyric Opera of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyric_Opera_of_Chicago "Lyric Opera of Chicago"). Bolcom, a teacher at the University of Michigan, had admired Altman's first production of _The Rake's Progress_ a decade prior and asked him for help adapting [Frank Norris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Norris "Frank Norris")'s [novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McTeague "McTeague").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-26) After finishing _Short Cuts_, Altman directed two episodes of _[Great Performances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great\_Performances "Great Performances")_. The first was an R&B revue; the second was a television adaptation of _McTeague_.

The rest of the 1990s saw limited success for Altman. His 1994 release _[Prêt-à-Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%AAt-%C3%A0-Porter\_(film) "Prêt-à-Porter (film)")_ (also known as _Ready to Wear_) garnered significant pre-release publicity, but was a commercial and critical flop, though it got several nominations for year-end awards, including two [Golden Globe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globes "Golden Globes") nominations and won the [National Board of Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Board_of_Review "National Board of Review") award for [Best Acting By An Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Board_of_Review_Award_for_Best_Cast "National Board of Review Award for Best Cast"). In 1996, Altman directed _[Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas\_City\_(1996\_film) "Kansas City (1996 film)")_, expressing his love of 1930s jazz through a complicated kidnapping story. Altman encouraged the film's on-set musicians to improvise, and unused footage of their performances formed the basis for Altman's third episode of _Great Performances_. The film received lukewarm-to-positive reviews, but made next to nothing at the box office, as did the 1998 legal thriller _[The Gingerbread Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Gingerbread\_Man\_(film) "The Gingerbread Man (film)")_. Though his 1997 anthology series _[Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun\_(TV\_series) "Gun (TV series)")_ had a high-profile cast, it was cancelled after only six episodes.

He did close the decade on a high note, with 1999's _[Cookie's Fortune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookie's\_Fortune "Cookie's Fortune")_, a quirky black comedy about the suicide of a wealthy dowager, his first film in almost 6 years to make back its budget, and which earned him generally positive praise from critics. He was elected a Fellow of the [American Academy of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Sciences "American Academy of Arts and Sciences") in 1999.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-AAAS-27) Though Altman's first film of the new millennium, _[Dr. T & the Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr.\_T\_&\_the\_Women "Dr. T & the Women")_, received only moderate reviews and middling financial success. His next film, _[Gosford Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosford\_Park "Gosford Park")_ (2001), was included on many critics' lists of the ten best films of that year. A large-cast, British country house [murder mystery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_mystery "Murder mystery"), it won the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay ([Julian Fellowes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Fellowes "Julian Fellowes")) plus six more nominations, including two for Altman, as Best Director and Best Picture.

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Robert_Altman%2C_director%2C_producer_LCCN2020729686.jpg/250px-Robert_Altman%2C_director%2C_producer_LCCN2020729686.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Altman,_director,_producer_LCCN2020729686.jpg)

Altman in 1980

Altman returned to the stage twice more. In 2004 He reunited with Bolcom, Weinstein, and the Lyric Opera to adapt his 1978 film, _A Wedding_, as an opera. It was generally well received.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-28) His final stage production was poorly received. In 2006, Altman travelled to England to direct the [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_theatre "West End theatre") debut of [Arthur Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Miller "Arthur Miller")'s final play, _[Resurrection Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection\_Blues "Resurrection Blues")_ at the [Old Vic Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Vic_Theatre "Old Vic Theatre"). At this time, the Old Vic was managed by [Kevin Spacey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Spacey "Kevin Spacey"), and the production starred [Maximilian Schell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilian_Schell "Maximilian Schell"), [James Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox "James Fox"), Neve Campbell, [Matthew Modine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Modine "Matthew Modine"), and [Jane Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Adams_(actress,_born_1965) "Jane Adams (actress, born 1965)"). However, despite the pedigree of all involved, the production was an abject failure with poor reviews and behind-the-scenes bickering.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-29)

Working with independent studios such as the now-shuttered Fine Line, Artisan (which was absorbed into today's [Lionsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lions_Gate_Entertainment "Lions Gate Entertainment")), and USA Films (now [Focus Features](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focus_Features "Focus Features")), gave Altman the edge in making the kinds of films he always wanted to make without studio interference. _[The Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Company\_(film) "The Company (film)")_, a film about the [Joffrey Ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joffrey_Ballet "Joffrey Ballet") in Chicago, featured a cast composed mainly of actual dancers. The film had been conceived by star [Neve Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neve_Campbell "Neve Campbell"), an ex ballerina, and written by Altman's longtime friend, [Barbara Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Turner_(screenwriter) "Barbara Turner (screenwriter)"). Altman directed a follow-up to _Tanner '88_ for the [Sundance Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundance_TV "Sundance TV"), reuniting him with [Michael Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Murphy_(actor) "Michael Murphy (actor)") as an older Jack Tanner. A [film version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Prairie_Home_Companion_(film) "A Prairie Home Companion (film)") of [Garrison Keillor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrison_Keillor "Garrison Keillor")'s public radio series _[A Prairie Home Companion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Prairie\_Home\_Companion "A Prairie Home Companion")_ was released in June 2006. Altman was still developing new projects up until his death, including a film based on _[Hands on a Hard Body: The Documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hands\_on\_a\_Hard\_Body:\_The\_Documentary "Hands on a Hard Body: The Documentary")_ (1997).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-30)

In 2006 the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") awarded Altman an [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") for Lifetime Achievement. During his acceptance speech he revealed that he had received a heart transplant approximately ten or eleven years earlier. The director then quipped that perhaps the academy had acted prematurely in recognizing the body of his work, as he felt like he might have four more decades of life ahead of him.

## Directing style and technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Directing style and technique")]

Altman's particular style of filmmaking covered many genres — referred to as _Altmanesque_[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-31) — but usually with a "[subversive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subversion "Subversion")" or "anti-Hollywood" twist which typically relied on [satire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire") and humor to express his personal views. Actors especially enjoyed working under his direction because he encouraged them to improvise. He preferred large [ensemble casts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_cast "Ensemble cast") for his films, and developed a [multitrack recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multitrack_recording "Multitrack recording") technique which produced overlapping dialogue from multiple actors. This produced a more natural, more dynamic, and more complex experience for the viewer. He also used highly mobile camera work and zoom lenses to enhance the activity taking place on the screen. Critic [Pauline Kael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Kael "Pauline Kael"), writing about his directing style, said that Altman could "make film fireworks out of next to nothing"[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Wakeman-32) and calls his method for making movies as "a step toward a new kind of movie naturalism."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-33)

### Maverick and auteur

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Maverick and auteur")]

Following his successful career in television, Altman began his new career in the film industry when he was in middle-age. He understood the creative limits imposed by the television medium, and now set out to direct and write films which would express his personal visions about American society and Hollywood. His films would later be described as "[auteuristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auteur "Auteur") attacks" and "idiosyncratic variations" of traditional films, typically using subtle comedy or satire as a way of expressing his observations.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Wakeman-32)

His films were typically related to political, ideological, and personal subjects, and Altman was known for "refusing to compromise his own artistic vision."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Hillstrom-34) He has been described as "anti-Hollywood," often ignoring the social pressures that affected others in the industry, which made it more difficult for him to get many of his films seen. He said his independence as a filmmaker helped him overall:

> I don't think there's a filmmaker alive, or who ever lived, who's had a better shake than I've had. I've never been without a project and it's always been a project of my own choosing. So I don't know how much better it could be. I have not become a mogul, I don't build castles and I don't have a vast personal fortune, but I have been able to do what I've wanted to do and I've done it a lot.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Stevens-35)

"Altman was a genuine movie maverick," states author [Ian Freer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Freer "Ian Freer"), because he went against the commercial conformity of the film industry: "He was the scourge of the film establishment, and his work generally cast an astute, scathing eye over the breadth of American culture, often exploding genres and character archetypes; Altman was fascinated by people with imperfections, people as they really are, not as the movies would have you believe."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Freer-36) Director [Alan Rudolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Rudolph "Alan Rudolph"), during a special tribute to Altman, refers to his moviemaking style as "Altmanesque."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-NYT-07-37)

With his independent style of directing, he developed a bad reputation among screenwriters and those on the business side of films. He admits, "I have a bad reputation with writers, developed over the years: 'Oh, he doesn't do what you write, blah blah blah.' ... [Ring Lardner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_Lardner,_Jr. "Ring Lardner, Jr.") was very pissed off with me," for not following his script.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Thompson-38):18 Nor did Altman get along well with studio heads, once punching an executive in the nose and knocking him into a swimming pool because he insisted he cut six minutes from a film he was working on.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Armstrong-39):9

His reputation among actors was better. With them, his independence sometimes extended to his choice of actors, often going against consensus. [Cher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cher "Cher"), for instance, credits him for launching her career with both the stage play and film, _[Come Back to the Five and Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come\_Back\_to\_the\_Five\_and\_Dime,\_Jimmy\_Dean,\_Jimmy\_Dean\_(film) "Come Back to the Five and Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean (film)")_ (1982). "Without Bob I would have never had a film career. Everyone told him not to cast me. Everyone. ... Nobody would give me a break. I am convinced that Bob was the only one who was brave enough to do it." Others, like [Julianne Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julianne_Moore "Julianne Moore"), describes working with him:

> You know, all this talk about Bob being this kind of irascible, difficult kind of person? Well, he was never that way with an actor or with a creative person that I saw. Never, never, never. He saved all that for the money people.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):431

Director [Robert Dornhelm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Dornhelm "Robert Dornhelm") said Altman "looked at film as a pure, artistic venue." With _[Short Cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short\_Cuts\_(film) "Short Cuts (film)")_ (1993), for instance, the distributor "begged him" to cut a few minutes from the length, to keep it commercially viable: "Bob just thought the antiChrist was trying to destroy his art. They were well-meaning people who wanted him to get what he deserved, which was a big commercial hit. But when it came down to the art or the money, he was with the art."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):438

[Sally Kellerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Kellerman "Sally Kellerman"), noting Altman's willful attitude, looked back with regret at giving up a chance to act in one of his films:

> I had just finished filming _[Last of the Red Hot Lovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last\_of\_the\_Red\_Hot\_Lovers "Last of the Red Hot Lovers")_ when Bob called me one day at home. "Sally, do you want to be in my picture after next?" he asked. "Only if it's a good part," I said. He hung up on me. Bob was as stubborn and arrogant as I was at the time, but the sad thing is that I cheated myself out of working with someone I loved so much, someone who made acting both fun and easy and who trusted his actors. Bob loved actors. Stars would line up to work for nothing for Bob Altman.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-41)

### Themes and subjects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Themes and subjects")]

Unlike directors whose work fits within various [film genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_genre "Film genre"), such as Westerns, musicals, war films, or comedies, Altman's work has been defined as more "anti-genre" by various critics.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Hillstrom-34) This is partly due to the satirical and comedy nature of many of his films. [Geraldine Chaplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Chaplin "Geraldine Chaplin"), daughter of [Charlie Chaplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Chaplin "Charlie Chaplin"), compared the humor in his films to her father's films:

> They're funny in the right way. Funny in a critical way — of what the world is and the world we live in. They were both geniuses in their way. They alter your experience of reality. They have their world and they have their humor. That humor is so rare.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):287

Altman made it clear that he did not like "storytelling" in his films, contrary to the way most television and mainstream film are made. According to Altman biographer [Mitchell Zuckoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitchell_Zuckoff "Mitchell Zuckoff"), "he disliked the word 'story,' believing that a plot should be secondary to an exploration of pure (or, even better, impure) human behavior."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):xiii Zuckoff describes the purposes underlying many of Altman's films: "He loved the chaotic nature of real life, with conflicting perspectives, surprising twists, unexplained actions, and ambiguous endings. He especially loved many voices, sometimes arguing, sometimes agreeing, ideally overlapping, a cocktail party or a street scene captured as he experienced it.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):xiii[Julianne Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julianne_Moore "Julianne Moore"), after seeing some of his movies, credits Altman's style of directing for her decision to become a film actress, rather than a stage actress:

> I felt it really strongly. And I thought, "I don't know who this guy is, but that's what I want to do. I want to do that kind of work." From then on I'd see his films whenever I could, and he was always my absolute favorite director, for what he said thematically and emotionally and how he felt about people.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):324

Film author Charles Derry writes that Altman's films "characteristically contain perceptive observations, telling exchanges, and moments of crystal clear revelation of human folly."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Hillstrom-34) Because Altman was an astute observer of society and "especially interested in people," notes Derry, many of his film characters had "that sloppy imperfection associated with human beings as they are, with life as it is lived."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Hillstrom-34) As a result, his films are often an indirect critique of American society.

The satirical content is evident In many of Altman's films: _[M*A*S*H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MASH\_(film) "MASH (film)")_ (1970), for example, is a satirical black comedy set during the Korean War; _[McCabe & Mrs. Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCabe\_&\_Mrs.\_Miller "McCabe & Mrs. Miller")_ (1971) is a satire on Westerns;[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Wood-42) author [Matthew Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Kennedy_(author) "Matthew Kennedy (author)") states that _[Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_(film) "Nashville (film)")_ (1975) is a "brilliant satire of America immediately prior to the Bicentennial";[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-43)_[A Wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Wedding\_(1978\_film) "A Wedding (1978 film)")_ (1978) is a satire on American marriage rituals and hypocrisy;[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-44) Altman himself said that _[The Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Player\_(1992\_film) "The Player (1992 film)")_ (1992) was "a very mild satire" about the Hollywood film industry, and [Vincent Canby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Canby "Vincent Canby") agreed, stating that "as a satire, _The Player_ tickles. It doesn't draw blood."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-45) The satire of his films sometimes led to their failure at the box office if their satirical nature was not understood by the distributor. Altman blames the box office failure of _[The Long Goodbye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Long\_Goodbye\_(film) "The Long Goodbye (film)")_ (1973), a detective story, on the erroneous marketing of the film as a thriller:

> When the picture opened, it was a big, big flop. ... I went to David Picker and said, "You can't do this. No wonder the fucking picture is failing. It's giving the wrong impression. You make it look like a thriller and it's not, it's a satire.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Thompson-38)

Similarly, Altman also blames the failure of _[O.C. & Stiggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O.C.\_&\_Stiggs "O.C. & Stiggs")_ on it being marketed as a typical "teenage movie," rather than what he filmed it as, a "satire of a teenage movie," he said.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Thompson-38)

### Improvisation dialogue

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Improvisation dialogue")]

Altman favored stories expressing the interrelationships among several characters, being more interested in character motivation than in intricate plots. He therefore tended to sketch out only a basic plot for the film, referring to the screenplay as a "blueprint" for action. By encouraging his actors to improvise dialogue, Altman thus became known as an "actor's director," a reputation that attracted many notable actors to work as part of his large casts. Performers enjoy working with Altman in part because "he provides them with the freedom to develop their characters and often alter the script through improvisation and collaboration," notes Derry. [Richard Baskin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Baskin "Richard Baskin") says that "Bob was rather extraordinary in his way of letting people do what they did. He trusted you to do what you did and therefore you would kill for him."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Hillstrom-34)

[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):282[Geraldine Chaplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Chaplin "Geraldine Chaplin"), who acted in _Nashville_, recalls one of her first rehearsal sessions:

> He said, "Have you brought your scripts?" We said yes. He said, "Well, throw them away. You don't need them. You need to know who you are and where you are and who you're with." ... It was like being onstage with a full house every second. All the circus acts you had inside your body you'd do just for him.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):282

Altman regularly let his actors develop a character through improvisation during rehearsal or sometimes during the actual filming.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Armstrong-39) Such improvisation was uncommon in film due to the high cost of film production which requires careful planning, precise scripts, and rehearsal, before costly film was exposed. Nevertheless, Altman preferred to use improvisation as a tool for helping his actors develop their character.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-46) Altman said that "once we start shooting it's a very set thing. Improvisation is misunderstood. We don't just turn people loose."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Stevens-35) Although he tried to avoid dictating an actor's every move, preferring to let them be in control:

> When I cast a film, most of my creative work is done. I have to be there to turn the switch on and give them encouragement as a father figure, but they do all the work. ... All I'm trying to do is make it easy on the actor, because once you start to shoot, the actor is the artist. ... I have to give them confidence and see that they have a certain amount of protection so they can be creative. ... I let them do what they became actors for in the first place: to create.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Stevens-35)

[Carol Burnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Burnett "Carol Burnett") remembers Altman admitting that many of the ideas in his films came from the actors. "You never hear a director say that. That was truly an astonishing thing," she said.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):328 Others, such as [Jennifer Jason Leigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Jason_Leigh "Jennifer Jason Leigh"), became creatively driven:

> He would inspire you out of sheer necessity to come up with stuff that you didn't know you were capable of, that you didn't know you had in you. He was so genuinely mischievous and so damn funny.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):435

Krin Gabbard adds that Altman enjoyed using actors "who flourish as improvisers," such as [Elliott Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott_Gould "Elliott Gould"), who starred in 5 of his films, including _M*A*S*H_, _The Long Goodbye_ and _California Split_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Armstrong-39) Gould recalls that when filming _M*A*S*H_, his first acting job with Altman, he and costar [Donald Sutherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Sutherland "Donald Sutherland") didn't think Altman knew what he was doing. He wrote years later, "I think that in hindsight, Donald and I were two elitist, arrogant actors who really weren't getting Altman's genius."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):174 Others in the cast immediately appreciated Altman's directing style. [René Auberjonois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Auberjonois "René Auberjonois") explains:

> We thought that's the way movies were. That they were that joyous an experience. If you had any kind of career, you quickly saw that most directors don't really trust actors, don't really want to see actors acting. That was the difference with Bob Altman. He loved actors and wanted to see acting.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):175

Unlike television and traditional films, Altman also avoided "conventional storytelling," and would opt for showing the "busy confusion of real life," observes Albert Lindauer.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Wakeman-32) Among the various techniques to achieve this effect, his films often include "a profusion of sounds and images, by huge casts or crazy characters, multiple plots or no plots at all, ... and a reliance on improvisation."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Wakeman-32) A few months before he died, Altman tried to summarize the motives behind his filmmaking style:

> I equate this work more with painting than with theater or literature. Stories don't interest me. Basically, I'm more interested in behavior. I don't direct, I watch. I have to be thrilled if I expect the audience to be thrilled. Because what I really want to see from an actor is something I've never seen before, so I can't tell them what it is. I try to encourage actors not to take turns. To deal with conversation as conversation. I mean, that's what the job is, I think. It's to make a comfort area so that an actor can go beyond what he thought he could do.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Zuckoff-40):8

### Sound techniques

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Sound techniques")]

Altman was one of the few filmmakers who "paid full attention to the possibilities of sound" when filming.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Freer-36) He tried to replicate natural conversational sounds, even with large casts, by wiring hidden microphones to actors, then recording them talking over each other with multiple soundtracks.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Freer-36) During the filming, he wore a headset to ensure that important dialogue could be heard, without emphasizing it. This produced a "dense audio experience" for viewers, allowing them to hear multiple scraps of dialogue, as if they were listening in on various private conversations. Altman recognized that although large casts hurt a film commercially, "I like to see a lot of stuff going on."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Stevens-35)

Altman first used overlapping soundtracks in _[M*A*S*H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MASH\_(film) "MASH (film)")_ (1970), a sound technique which film author Michael Barson describes as "a breathtaking innovation at the time."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Barson-47) He developed it, Altman said, to force viewers to pay attention and become engaged in the film as if they were an active participant.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Wakeman-32) According to some critics, one of the more extreme uses of the technique is in _[McCabe and Mrs. Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCabe\_and\_Mrs.\_Miller "McCabe and Mrs. Miller")_ (1971), also considered among his finest films.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Hillstrom-34)

Film historian/scholar [Robert P. Kolker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_P._Kolker "Robert P. Kolker") pointed out that the aural and visual simultaneity in Altman's films was critical as that represented an emphasis on the plurality of events, which required viewers to become active spectators.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-48)

### Ensemble casts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Ensemble casts")]

Overlapping dialogue among large groups of actors adds complexity to Altman's films, and they were often criticized as appearing haphazard or disconnected on first viewing. Some of his critics changed their minds after seeing them again. British film critic [David Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Thomson_(film_critic) "David Thomson (film critic)") gave _[Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_(film) "Nashville (film)")_ (1975) a bad review after watching it the first time, but later wrote, "But going back to _Nashville_ and some of the earlier films, ... made me reflect: It remains enigmatic how organized or purposeful _Nashville_ is. ... The mosaic, or mix, permits a freedom and a human idiosyncrasy that [Renoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Renoir "Jean Renoir") might have admired."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Thomson-49) During the making of the film, the actors were inspired, and co-star [Ronee Blakley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronee_Blakley "Ronee Blakley") was convinced of the film's ultimate success:

> Yes, I did think it was going to be great, all the work was so good, every actor was inspired, and Altman's team was intensely competent, and he was that rare kind of genius who knows what works and what doesn't at the moment it is happening.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-50)

Thomson later recognized those aspects as being part of Altman's style, beginning with _[M*A*S*H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MASH\_(film) "MASH (film)")_ (1970): "_MASH_ began to develop the crucial Altman style of overlapping, blurred sound and images so slippery with zoom that there was no sense of composition. That is what makes _Nashville_ so absorbing."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Thomson-49) Altman explained that to him such overlapping dialogue in his films was closer to reality, especially with large groups: "If you've got fourteen people at a dinner table, it seems to me it's pretty unlikely that only two of them are going to be talking."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Stevens-35)[Pauline Kael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Kael "Pauline Kael") writes that Altman, "the master of large ensembles, loose action, and overlapping voices, demonstrates that ... he can make film fireworks out of next to nothing."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Wakeman-32)

### Photography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Photography")]

Altman's distinctive style of directing carried over into his preferences for camerawork. Among them was his use of widescreen compositions, intended to capture the many people or activities taking place on screen at the same time. For some films, such as _McCabe and Mrs. Miller_, he created a powerful visual atmosphere with cinematographer [Vilmos Zsigmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilmos_Zsigmond "Vilmos Zsigmond"), such as scenes using fluid camerawork, zoom lenses, and a smoky effect using special fog filters.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Frost-51) Director [Stanley Kubrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kubrick "Stanley Kubrick") told Altman that "the camerawork was wonderful," and asked, "How did you do it?"[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Rogers-52)

In _Nashville_, Altman used sets with noticeable colors of reds, whites and blues. For _The Long Goodbye_, he insisted that Zsigmond keep the camera mobile by mounting it to moving objects.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Hillstrom-34) Zsigmond states that Altman "wanted to do something different" in this film, and told him he "wanted the camera to move — all the time. Up. down. In and out. Side to side."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Rogers-52) Cinematographer [Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins"), discussing his use of zoom lenses, commented, "I would find it quite exciting to shoot a film with a zoom lens if it was that observational, roving kind of look that Robert Altman was known for. He'd put the camera on a jib arm and float across the scene and pick out these shots as he went along – quite a nice way of working."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Frost-51)

Zsigmond also recalls that working with Altman was fun:

> We rather enjoyed doing things "improv." Altman is a great improviser. During the first few days of the shoot, he would "create" different approaches on a moment's notice. He would show me how he wanted the camera to move — always move. Which was fun. The actors loved it, and I was always challenged to find ways to shoot what Altman came up with.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Rogers-52)

Vilmos Zsigmond's cinematography in _McCabe and Mrs. Miller_ received a nomination by the [British Academy Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Awards "British Academy Film Awards").

### Music scores

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Music scores")]

When using music in his films, Altman was known to be highly selective, often choosing music that he personally liked. Director [Paul Thomas Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Thomas_Anderson "Paul Thomas Anderson"), who worked with him, notes that "Altman's use of music is always important," adding, "Bob loved his music, didn't he? My God, he loved his music".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Armstrong-39) Since he was a "great fan" of [Leonard Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Cohen "Leonard Cohen")'s music, for example, saying he would "just get stoned and play that stuff" all the time[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Thompson-38) he used three of his songs in _[McCabe and Mrs. Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCabe\_and\_Mrs.\_Miller "McCabe and Mrs. Miller")_ (1971), and another for the final scene in _[A Wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Wedding\_(1978\_film) "A Wedding (1978 film)")_ (1978).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-53)

For _[Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_(film) "Nashville (film)")_ (1975), Altman had numerous new country music songs written by his cast to create a realistic atmosphere. He incorporated a "hauntingly repeated melody" in _[The Long Goodbye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Long\_Goodbye\_(film) "The Long Goodbye (film)")_ (1973), and employed [Harry Nilsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Nilsson "Harry Nilsson") and [Van Dyke Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Dyke_Parks "Van Dyke Parks") to score _[Popeye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popeye\_(film) "Popeye (film)")_ (1980).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-McGilligan-18):347

A number of music experts have written about Altman's use of music, including Richard R. Ness, who wrote about the scores for many of Altman's films in an article, considered to be a valuable resource for understanding Altman's filmmaking technique.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-54) Similarly, cinema studies professor Krin Gabbard[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-55) wrote an analysis of Altman's use of jazz music in _[Short Cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short\_Cuts\_(film) "Short Cuts (film)")_ (1993), noting that few critics have considered the "importance of the music" in the film.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Armstrong-39)

Jazz was also significant in _[Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas\_City\_(1996\_film) "Kansas City (1996 film)")_ (1996). In that film, the music is considered to be the basis of the story. Altman states that "the whole idea was not to be too specific about the story," but to have the film itself be "rather a sort of jazz."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Self-56) Altman's technique of making the theme of a film a form of music, was considered "an experiment nobody has tried before," with Altman admitting it was risky. "I didn't know if it would work. ... If people 'get it,' then they really tend to like it."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-Altman-57)

Altman gave several directors, including [Alan Rudolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Rudolph "Alan Rudolph"), [Reza Badiyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reza_Badiyi "Reza Badiyi"), and [Richard C. ## Frequent collaborators

**Robert Bernard Altman** ([/ˈ ɔː l t m ə n/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_AWLT-mən_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-1) February 20, 1925 – November 20, 2006) was an American filmmaker. He is considered an enduring figure from the [New Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hollywood "New Hollywood") era, known for directing [subversive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subversive "Subversive") and [satirical films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire") with overlapping dialogue and [ensemble casts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_cast "Ensemble cast"). Over [his career](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman_filmography "Robert Altman filmography") he received [numerous accolades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Robert_Altman "List of awards and nominations received by Robert Altman"), including an [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award"), two [BAFTAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Awards "British Academy Film Awards"), three [Independent Spirit Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Spirit_Awards "Independent Spirit Awards"), a [Primetime Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Awards "Primetime Emmy Awards"), a [David di Donatello Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_di_Donatello_Award "David di Donatello Award"), and a [Golden Globe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Awards "Golden Globe Awards"), as well as nominations for seven competitive [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards").

Altman was nominated for five [Academy Awards for Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") for the [war comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_comedy "War comedy")_[M*A*S*H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M*A*S*H\_(film) "M*A*S*H (film)")_ (1970), the [musical film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_film "Musical film")_[Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville\_(film) "Nashville (film)")_ (1975), the [Hollywood satire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire")_[The Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Player\_(1992\_film) "The Player (1992 film)")_ (1992), the [dark comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_comedy "Dark comedy")_[Short Cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short\_Cuts "Short Cuts")_ (1993), and the [murder mystery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_mystery "Murder mystery")_[Gosford Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosford\_Park "Gosford Park")_ (2001). He is also known for directing _[Brewster McCloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster\_McCloud "Brewster McCloud")_ (1970), _[McCabe & Mrs. Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCabe\_&\_Mrs.\_Miller "McCabe & Mrs. Miller")_ (1971), _[The Long Goodbye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Long\_Goodbye\_(film) "The Long Goodbye (film)")_ (1973), _[California Split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California\_Split "California Split")_ (1974), _[Thieves Like Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thieves\_Like\_Us\_(film) "Thieves Like Us (film)")_ (1974), _[3 Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3\_Women "3 Women")_ (1977), _[A Wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Wedding\_(1978\_film) "A Wedding (1978 film)")_ (1978), _[Popeye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popeye\_(film) "Popeye (film)")_ (1980), _[Secret Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret\_Honor "Secret Honor")_ (1984), _[The Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Company\_(film) "The Company (film)")_ (2003), and _[A Prairie Home Companion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Prairie\_Home\_Companion\_(film) "A Prairie Home Companion (film)")_ (2006).

Also known for his work on television, he directed the [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO")[political](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics "Politics")[mockumentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mockumentary "Mockumentary") miniseries _[Tanner '88](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanner\_'88 "Tanner '88")_ (1988) for which he won the [Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Directing_for_a_Drama_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series"). He also directed the HBO television film _[The Laundromat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Laundromat\_(1985\_film) "The Laundromat (1985 film)")_ (1985). On stage, he directed the [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(theatre) "Broadway (theatre)") revival of the [Ed Graczyk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Graczyk "Ed Graczyk") play _[Come Back to the 5 & Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come\_Back\_to\_the\_5\_&\_Dime,\_Jimmy\_Dean,\_Jimmy\_Dean\_(play) "Come Back to the 5 & Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean (play)")_ (1981) and later the [1982 film of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come_Back_to_the_5_&_Dime,_Jimmy_Dean,_Jimmy_Dean_(film) "Come Back to the 5 & Dime, Jimmy Dean, Jimmy Dean (film)"). He directed the [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_(theatre) "West End (theatre)") revival of [Arthur Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Miller "Arthur Miller")'s [penultimate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penultimate "Penultimate") play _[Resurrection Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection\_Blues "Resurrection Blues")_ (2006).

In 2006, the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") recognized Altman's body of work with an [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award"). He died that same year at the age of 81. Despite seven nominations, Altman never won a competitive Academy Award. His films _M*A*S*H_, _McCabe & Mrs. Miller_, _The Long Goodbye_ and _Nashville_ have been selected for the United States [National Film Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Registry "National Film Registry"). Altman is also one of five filmmakers whose films have won the [Golden Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Bear "Golden Bear") at [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_International_Film_Festival "Berlin International Film Festival"), the [Golden Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion") at [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Film_Festival "Venice Film Festival"), and the [Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or") at [Cannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") (the other four being [Henri-Georges Clouzot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Georges_Clouzot "Henri-Georges Clouzot"), [Michelangelo Antonioni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo_Antonioni "Michelangelo Antonioni"), [Jean-Luc Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Godard "Jean-Luc Godard") and [Jafar Panahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jafar_Panahi "Jafar Panahi")).

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Altman&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Altman was born on February 20, 1925, in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"), the son of Helen (née Matthews), a _[Mayflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayflower "Mayflower")_ descendant from [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska"), and Bernard Clement Altman, a wealthy insurance salesman and amateur gambler who came from an upper-class family. Altman's ancestry was German, English and Irish;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-altman3-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-altman1-3) his paternal grandfather, Frank Altman Sr., anglicized the spelling of the family name from "Altmann" to "Altman".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-altman1-3) Altman had a [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic") upbringing,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-altman2-4) but he did not continue to follow or practice the religion as an adult,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-5) although he has been referred to as "a sort of Catholic" and a Catholic director.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-altman2-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-6) He was educated at [Jesuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit "Jesuit") schools, including [Rockhurst High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockhurst_High_School "Rockhurst High School"), in Kansas City.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-7) He graduated from [Wentworth Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wentworth_Military_Academy "Wentworth Military Academy") in [Lexington, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington,_Missouri "Lexington, Missouri") in 1943.

Soon after graduation, Altman joined the [United States Army Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces "United States Army Air Forces") at the age of 18. During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), he flew more than 50 bombing missions as a co-pilot of a [B-24 Liberator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consolidated_B-24_Liberator "Consolidated B-24 Liberator") with the [307th Bomb Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/307th_Operations_Group "307th Operations Group") in [Borneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borneo "Borneo") and the [Dutch East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_Indies "Dutch East Indies").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-altm-9) Upon his discharge in 1947 he moved to California. He worked in publicity for a company that had invented a tattooing machine to identify dogs. He entered filmmaking on a whim, selling a script to [RKO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RKO "RKO") for the 1948 picture _[Bodyguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodyguard\_(1948\_film) "Bodyguard (1948 film)")_, which he co-wrote with George W. George. Altman's immediate success encouraged him to move to New York City, where he attempted to forge a career as a writer. Having enjoyed little success, he returned to Kansas City in 1949 and accepted a job as a director and writer of industrial films for the [Calvin Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Company "Calvin Company"). He directed some 65 industrial films and documentaries for the Calvin Company. Through his early work on industrial films, he experimented with narrative technique and developed his characteristic use of overlapping dialogue. In February 2012, an early Calvin film directed by Altman, _Modern Football_ (1951), was found by filmmaker Gary Huggins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-11)

Altman also had a career directing plays and operas parallel to his film career. While he was employed by the Calvin Company he began directing plays at the Resident Theatre of the Jewish Community Center. These plays allowed him to work with local actors, such as fellow future director [Richard C. Sarafian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_C._Sarafian "Richard C. Sarafian"), whom he directed in a production of Richard Harrity's _Hope Is the Thing with Feathers_. Sarafian would later marry Altman's sister and follow him to Hollywood.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman#cite_note-12)
