## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Baseline_Drive-in_Ad_-_27_March_1957%2C_Highland%2C_CA.jpg/250px-Baseline_Drive-in_Ad_-_27_March_1957%2C_Highland%2C_CA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baseline_Drive-in_Ad_-_27_March_1957,_Highland,_CA.jpg)

[Drive-in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-in_theater "Drive-in theater") advertisement from 1957 for _The Delinquents_ and co-feature, _[Hit and Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit\_and\_Run\_(1957\_film) "Hit and Run (1957 film)")_.

Elmer Rhoden Jr. was a Kansas City motion picture theater exhibitor, president of the prominent Commonwealth Theaters chain in [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), and [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota"). Rhoden wanted to get into producing films. He had the distributing apparatus at hand and the necessary capital to invest. Although television was drawing viewers out of the theaters, teenagers still frequented theaters, and, soon, film producers realized that there was a large "teen market" they could tap into. During the mid-to-late 1950s, following the success of movies by [American International Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_International_Pictures "American International Pictures") aimed at the teenage market such as _[Shake, Rattle & Rock!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake,\_Rattle\_&\_Rock!\_(1956\_film) "Shake, Rattle & Rock! (1956 film)")_ and _[Hot Rod Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot\_Rod\_Girl "Hot Rod Girl"),_ a huge wave of films, often referred to as [exploitation films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploitation_film "Exploitation film"), were later produced by the major [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") studios and independents alike. Common subjects of 1950s teen films included [juvenile delinquency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenile_delinquency "Juvenile delinquency"), [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll"), [horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_(emotion) "Horror (emotion)"), [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction"), and [hot rods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_rods "Hot rods"). Rhoden Jr. was one of the first independent exhibitors to note these shifts in the film industry and was determined to make it work for his business.

Due to the "consent decree" component of the ["Paramount Ruling"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Paramount_Pictures,_Inc. "United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc."), the major studios were constrained from booking their own chains by this [antitrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antitrust "Antitrust") ruling. But the Commonwealth circuit and other small regional independent film companies, by virtue of not having previously existed as film producers, were exempt from this rule. It was the beginning of the days of the low-budget regional filmmaker, and Rhoden figured that if he budgeted his "teen-flicks" cheaply enough and peddled them to his own Commonwealth chain, he would be guaranteed a tidy profit. So, in the spring of 1956, he raised $63,000 with the help of other local businessmen in Kansas City, decided his first teen film would be about troubled teens, thought up a title for it and nothing else, and hired local filmmaker Robert Altman (who knew Rhoden Jr. casually and had been directing industrial films and documentaries for the local [Calvin Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Company "Calvin Company")) to write and direct the film.

Using several starting points such as _[Blackboard Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackboard\_Jungle "Blackboard Jungle")_, _[The Wild One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wild\_One "The Wild One")_, and _[Rebel Without a Cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel\_Without\_a\_Cause "Rebel Without a Cause")_ for influence, Altman wrote the screenplay for _The Delinquents_ in five to seven days.

### Casting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Casting")]

Rhoden approved the script and gave Altman the go-ahead on the casting, scouting of locations, and so forth. For much of the cast, Altman turned to the local Kansas City actors with whom he had worked in community theater and in industrial films, including James Lantz, Leonard Belove, and Kermit Echols, as well as his then-wife Lotus Corelli and his eight-year-old daughter Christine. However, hoping for a [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States")-style film, Altman and Rhoden took a trip to [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") and cast for the three leads there. They came up with Peter Miller from _Blackboard Jungle_ to play Cholly, and Richard Bakalyan to play Eddy. [Tom Laughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Laughlin "Tom Laughlin") was cast in the lead role of Scotty, here making his film debut. Altman and Rhoden also came back from California with soundman Bob Post and camera operator Harry Birch.

Altman employed his friends and Calvin co-workers on the crew, including [Reza Badiyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reza_Badiyi "Reza Badiyi") as assistant director/associate producer and his sister Joan as production manager. Altman scouted locations in Kansas City and chose to film in Loose Park, as well as at the Jewel Box Nightclub, one of his favorite hangouts, and also at several popular local teen hangouts including the Crest Drive-In Theater (which Rhoden owned) and Allen's Drive-In. Through Kansas City native George Kuhn, one of the actors in the teenage gang in the film, Altman secured the temporary use of two houses to be those of Scotty and Janice in the film. One of them was Kuhn's and his parents', the other was his neighbors'.

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")]

Altman filmed _The Delinquents_ in three weeks during the summer of 1956. Although Rhoden was officially the executive producer, Altman did most of that type of work himself. As Altman said years later, "I wrote the thing in five days, cast it, picked the locations, drove the generator truck, got the people together, took no money, and we just did it, that's all". Altman had the cooperation of local businesses as well as the Kansas City Police Department. Altman and Rhoden had actually gone to the police to make sure their portrayal of delinquents and their problems was accurate, and also contacted them in order to receive their cooperation for blocking off streets and using the police station for certain scenes. They also used real police officers as actors in the film.

Altman's film crew was made up mostly of his Calvin co-workers. Calvin photographer Charles Paddock was director of photography, and Badiyi was assistant director. Calvin artist and designer (and Altman's brother-in-law) Chet Allen was art director, and Altman's sister Joan served in a production executive (such as script girl) while Altman's wife (Lotus Corelli) and daughter Christine also starred in the film. Also with Altman's Kansas City crew were Californians Harry Birch (camera operator) and Bob Post (sound recorder).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-3)

Laughlin was cast after Altman consulted the only agent he had in Bob Longnecker, who had Laughlin as a client.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-4) Laughlin and Altman had conflicting theories of acting. To Altman, Laughlin was "an unbelievable pain in the ass", guilty that he had not become a priest, "with a big Catholic hangup and a [James Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dean "James Dean") complex". There was one particular incident where Altman was ready to shoot a scene in which Laughlin was supposed to appear physically exhausted, and Laughlin excused himself with, "I've got to get in the mood now". Laughlin then insisted on running around the block a couple of times while cast and crew cooled their heels. Laughlin was attempting to do "everything he'd heard about James Dean doing", but when Laughlin's attempts at [method acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_acting "Method acting") were not welcomed by the rest of the cast or crew, he wanted to quit the film. Altman then worked out a compromise for communication whereby Altman would tell Laughlin exactly what he wanted in any given scene. According to Altman, Laughlin "performed the last half of the picture under protest".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-5) Laughlin, who described himself not as a Method actor but a "Stanislavsky actor", described the production as "very amateurish", disapproving of the lack of organization in Altman, with one instance involving Laughlin deciding to roll the cameras himself and shoot a scene rather than wait for Altman to show up for the crew (as he felt guilt over the fact that the production was on Rhoden’s money), which began the seeds of Laughlin starting to become a director.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-6)

Altman's experimental directing style was still developing, but one sign of his future directorial achievements can be seen in a story told by one of Altman's young cast members, [SuEllen Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SuEllen_Fried "SuEllen Fried"), about the shooting of a party scene in the film: "He rented an old house off Walworth Boulevard and told us to pretend we were having the wildest party of our lives, while he moved the camera from room to room and just filmed whatever was going on. We didn't know when the camera was going. We were just having a wild party". Altman (who described writing the film as one done over a weekend that he dictated to his sister Joan that would see the scenes improvised on set) expressed his thoughts about doing a script as one where he tried to avoid the characters having the same voice, where the distinction in sources and voices seemed closer to reality that would push the actor into creating the part rather than having the writer or director just bring the elements prepackaged, which only works out if the actor is willing to take the responsibility.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-7)

### Post-production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Post-production")]

Finally, _The Delinquents_ has also been noted (and praised) for its "technical excellence", particularly the quality of the [black-and-white photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-and-white_photography "Black-and-white photography"). Director of photography Charles Paddock said that, just before beginning filming on _The Delinquents_, Altman advised him to watch the film _[The Asphalt Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Asphalt\_Jungle "The Asphalt Jungle")_ and imitate that style of lighting.

The filming was completed by August 1956. In his contract with Rhoden, Altman had a clause stipulating that the film's post-production and editing would be executed under professional conditions in Hollywood. In late August, Altman and Reza Badiyi traveled across the country by car (Rhoden would not approve the air fare) to edit the film in California with Helene Turner. [Fred Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Brown_(sound_editor) "Frederick Brown (sound editor)") contributed the sound effects.

The finished film was picked up for distribution by [United Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists "United Artists") for $150,000, who wanted a teenage exploitation film in order to compete with the other studios. United Artists altered the ending a bit and added a moralistic narration by a stock actor at the beginning and end. Altman did not find out until he saw a preview of the film, and was not impressed.

## Release and legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Release and legacy")]

_The Delinquents_ received its "[gala world premiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_premiere "Film premiere")" in Kansas City in February 1957. The showing of the film was preceded by live music, a dance contest, and a parade of [Corvettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet_Corvette "Chevrolet Corvette") carrying residents who had worked on the film. It was all covered by a live radio broadcast and the theater's house lights were brought out.

The film was rejected by the [British Board of Film Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Board_of_Film_Classification "British Board of Film Classification") in 1957.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-8) United Artists released the film worldwide the next month. The film's release was not wide, and it played mostly in drive-ins. However, it did gross $1,000,000 for United Artists. When [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock") saw the film, he was apparently impressed enough to give Altman a job directing episodes of _[Alfred Hitchcock Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred\_Hitchcock\_Presents "Alfred Hitchcock Presents")_, which led to more television work for Altman over the next decade.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-9)

Rhoden produced one more film in Kansas City (_[The Cool and the Crazy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cool\_and\_the\_Crazy "The Cool and the Crazy")_) and was featured in [_TIME_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_magazine "Time magazine") as one of the "new wave" of producers. He then produced a delinquency film in Hollywood, _[Daddy-O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daddy-O\_(film) "Daddy-O (film)")_, but his mini-mogul reign was short-lived. An alcoholic who drank heavily, he died in 1959 at the age of 37 three months after suffering a heart attack.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-11)

_**The Delinquents**_ is a 1957 American [drama film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)") written, produced, and directed by Robert Altman.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-1) As the directorial debut of Altman, he filmed it in his hometown of [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri") during the summer of 1956 on a $63,000 budget (equivalent to $746,000 in 2025).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-inflation-US-2) It is not only the first film Altman directed, but also the first to star [Tom Laughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Laughlin "Tom Laughlin").

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

In suburban Kansas City, a group of hot-rod [greasers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greaser_(subculture) "Greaser (subculture)") and carousing delinquents stir trouble in a bar when they are denied drinks. Cholly and Eddy, the leaders of the gang, respond by breaking a window. Meanwhile, 18-year-old Scotty White and 16-year-old Janice Wilson are very much in love, but her parents stand between them because Janice is "too young to go steady" and Scotty "hangs out with the wrong crowd", with her dad telling him to stay away. Scotty, going to college in the fall, is told he could talk to them about seeing her when he comes back for Christmas vacation. At the drive-in alone that night, Scotty gets wrongly targeted by a gang who are looking for the person who slashed one of their tires. Cholly comes to Scotty's rescue. Cholly cooks up the idea of posing as Janice's new boyfriend and bringing her to meet Scotty the next night. The plan works well, and the teen crowd all meet at an abandoned mansion on the edge of town. However, the party gets out of hand with wild drinking and dancing, and Scotty and Janice leave to be alone after Cholly and Eddy each dance suggestively with Janice.

Soon after, the police mysteriously appear and break up the drunken free-for-all. Cholly and his right-hand-delinquent Eddy suspect Scotty of tipping off the police, and the whole gang kidnaps Scotty the next day and force him to gulp down an entire bottle of Scotch when he won't admit to being the informant. In panic after Scotty passes out from drinking, the gang begins to drive him out to the country with the intention of abandoning him on the side of the road but on the way they pull into a service station to get some gas. Eddy decides to hold up the station, but Scotty unknowingly bungles it when he wakes up. Cholly hits the station attendant on the head with a gas pump, and the gang speeds off, leaving Scotty behind with the cash and the attendant. Scotty staggers home, finds the gang has kidnapped Janice, has several fights, and then has a switchblade fight with Cholly (told by a psychotic Eddy to kill Scotty to kill the only witness) in a home kitchen. Wounded, Scotty then goes to the police as the Whites and Wilsons reclaim their kids.

The film, which had started with a voiceover describing it as a tale of violence and immorality, ends with a voiceover:

> “This is one story. Who's to blame? The answers are not easy, nor are they pleasant. We are all responsible, and it's our responsibility not to look the other way. Violence and immorality like this must be controlled, channeled. Citizens everywhere must work against delinquency, just as they work against cancer, cerebral palsy, or any other crippling disease. For delinquency is a disease. But the remedies are available: patience, compassion, understanding, and respect for parental and civil authority. By working with your church group, with a youth organization in your town, by paying closer attention to the needs of your children, you can help prevent the recurrence of regrettable events like the ones you have just witnessed. You can help halt the disease before it cripples our children, before it cripples society.”

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Baseline_Drive-in_Ad_-_27_March_1957%2C_Highland%2C_CA.jpg/250px-Baseline_Drive-in_Ad_-_27_March_1957%2C_Highland%2C_CA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baseline_Drive-in_Ad_-_27_March_1957,_Highland,_CA.jpg)

[Drive-in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-in_theater "Drive-in theater") advertisement from 1957 for _The Delinquents_ and co-feature, _[Hit and Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit\_and\_Run\_(1957\_film) "Hit and Run (1957 film)")_.

Elmer Rhoden Jr. was a Kansas City motion picture theater exhibitor, president of the prominent Commonwealth Theaters chain in [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), and [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota"). Rhoden wanted to get into producing films. He had the distributing apparatus at hand and the necessary capital to invest. Although television was drawing viewers out of the theaters, teenagers still frequented theaters, and, soon, film producers realized that there was a large "teen market" they could tap into. During the mid-to-late 1950s, following the success of movies by [American International Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_International_Pictures "American International Pictures") aimed at the teenage market such as _[Shake, Rattle & Rock!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake,\_Rattle\_&\_Rock!\_(1956\_film) "Shake, Rattle & Rock! (1956 film)")_ and _[Hot Rod Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot\_Rod\_Girl "Hot Rod Girl"),_ a huge wave of films, often referred to as [exploitation films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploitation_film "Exploitation film"), were later produced by the major [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") studios and independents alike. Common subjects of 1950s teen films included [juvenile delinquency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenile_delinquency "Juvenile delinquency"), [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll"), [horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_(emotion) "Horror (emotion)"), [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction"), and [hot rods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_rods "Hot rods"). Rhoden Jr. was one of the first independent exhibitors to note these shifts in the film industry and was determined to make it work for his business.

Due to the "consent decree" component of the ["Paramount Ruling"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Paramount_Pictures,_Inc. "United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc."), the major studios were constrained from booking their own chains by this [antitrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antitrust "Antitrust") ruling. But the Commonwealth circuit and other small regional independent film companies, by virtue of not having previously existed as film producers, were exempt from this rule. It was the beginning of the days of the low-budget regional filmmaker, and Rhoden figured that if he budgeted his "teen-flicks" cheaply enough and peddled them to his own Commonwealth chain, he would be guaranteed a tidy profit. So, in the spring of 1956, he raised $63,000 with the help of other local businessmen in Kansas City, decided his first teen film would be about troubled teens, thought up a title for it and nothing else, and hired local filmmaker Robert Altman (who knew Rhoden Jr. casually and had been directing industrial films and documentaries for the local [Calvin Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Company "Calvin Company")) to write and direct the film.

Using several starting points such as _[Blackboard Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackboard\_Jungle "Blackboard Jungle")_, _[The Wild One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wild\_One "The Wild One")_, and _[Rebel Without a Cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel\_Without\_a\_Cause "Rebel Without a Cause")_ for influence, Altman wrote the screenplay for _The Delinquents_ in five to seven days.

### Casting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Casting")]

Rhoden approved the script and gave Altman the go-ahead on the casting, scouting of locations, and so forth. For much of the cast, Altman turned to the local Kansas City actors with whom he had worked in community theater and in industrial films, including James Lantz, Leonard Belove, and Kermit Echols, as well as his then-wife Lotus Corelli and his eight-year-old daughter Christine. However, hoping for a [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States")-style film, Altman and Rhoden took a trip to [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") and cast for the three leads there. They came up with Peter Miller from _Blackboard Jungle_ to play Cholly, and Richard Bakalyan to play Eddy. [Tom Laughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Laughlin "Tom Laughlin") was cast in the lead role of Scotty, here making his film debut. Altman and Rhoden also came back from California with soundman Bob Post and camera operator Harry Birch.

Altman employed his friends and Calvin co-workers on the crew, including [Reza Badiyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reza_Badiyi "Reza Badiyi") as assistant director/associate producer and his sister Joan as production manager. Altman scouted locations in Kansas City and chose to film in Loose Park, as well as at the Jewel Box Nightclub, one of his favorite hangouts, and also at several popular local teen hangouts including the Crest Drive-In Theater (which Rhoden owned) and Allen's Drive-In. Through Kansas City native George Kuhn, one of the actors in the teenage gang in the film, Altman secured the temporary use of two houses to be those of Scotty and Janice in the film. One of them was Kuhn's and his parents', the other was his neighbors'.

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")]

Altman filmed _The Delinquents_ in three weeks during the summer of 1956. Although Rhoden was officially the executive producer, Altman did most of that type of work himself. As Altman said years later, "I wrote the thing in five days, cast it, picked the locations, drove the generator truck, got the people together, took no money, and we just did it, that's all". Altman had the cooperation of local businesses as well as the Kansas City Police Department. Altman and Rhoden had actually gone to the police to make sure their portrayal of delinquents and their problems was accurate, and also contacted them in order to receive their cooperation for blocking off streets and using the police station for certain scenes. They also used real police officers as actors in the film.

Altman's film crew was made up mostly of his Calvin co-workers. Calvin photographer Charles Paddock was director of photography, and Badiyi was assistant director. Calvin artist and designer (and Altman's brother-in-law) Chet Allen was art director, and Altman's sister Joan served in a production executive (such as script girl) while Altman's wife (Lotus Corelli) and daughter Christine also starred in the film. Also with Altman's Kansas City crew were Californians Harry Birch (camera operator) and Bob Post (sound recorder).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-3)

Laughlin was cast after Altman consulted the only agent he had in Bob Longnecker, who had Laughlin as a client.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-4) Laughlin and Altman had conflicting theories of acting. To Altman, Laughlin was "an unbelievable pain in the ass", guilty that he had not become a priest, "with a big Catholic hangup and a [James Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dean "James Dean") complex". There was one particular incident where Altman was ready to shoot a scene in which Laughlin was supposed to appear physically exhausted, and Laughlin excused himself with, "I've got to get in the mood now". Laughlin then insisted on running around the block a couple of times while cast and crew cooled their heels. Laughlin was attempting to do "everything he'd heard about James Dean doing", but when Laughlin's attempts at [method acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_acting "Method acting") were not welcomed by the rest of the cast or crew, he wanted to quit the film. Altman then worked out a compromise for communication whereby Altman would tell Laughlin exactly what he wanted in any given scene. According to Altman, Laughlin "performed the last half of the picture under protest".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-5) Laughlin, who described himself not as a Method actor but a "Stanislavsky actor", described the production as "very amateurish", disapproving of the lack of organization in Altman, with one instance involving Laughlin deciding to roll the cameras himself and shoot a scene rather than wait for Altman to show up for the crew (as he felt guilt over the fact that the production was on Rhoden’s money), which began the seeds of Laughlin starting to become a director.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-6)

Altman's experimental directing style was still developing, but one sign of his future directorial achievements can be seen in a story told by one of Altman's young cast members, [SuEllen Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SuEllen_Fried "SuEllen Fried"), about the shooting of a party scene in the film: "He rented an old house off Walworth Boulevard and told us to pretend we were having the wildest party of our lives, while he moved the camera from room to room and just filmed whatever was going on. We didn't know when the camera was going. We were just having a wild party". Altman (who described writing the film as one done over a weekend that he dictated to his sister Joan that would see the scenes improvised on set) expressed his thoughts about doing a script as one where he tried to avoid the characters having the same voice, where the distinction in sources and voices seemed closer to reality that would push the actor into creating the part rather than having the writer or director just bring the elements prepackaged, which only works out if the actor is willing to take the responsibility.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-7)

### Post-production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Post-production")]

Finally, _The Delinquents_ has also been noted (and praised) for its "technical excellence", particularly the quality of the [black-and-white photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-and-white_photography "Black-and-white photography"). Director of photography Charles Paddock said that, just before beginning filming on _The Delinquents_, Altman advised him to watch the film _[The Asphalt Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Asphalt\_Jungle "The Asphalt Jungle")_ and imitate that style of lighting.

The filming was completed by August 1956. In his contract with Rhoden, Altman had a clause stipulating that the film's post-production and editing would be executed under professional conditions in Hollywood. In late August, Altman and Reza Badiyi traveled across the country by car (Rhoden would not approve the air fare) to edit the film in California with Helene Turner. [Fred Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Brown_(sound_editor) "Frederick Brown (sound editor)") contributed the sound effects.

The finished film was picked up for distribution by [United Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists "United Artists") for $150,000, who wanted a teenage exploitation film in order to compete with the other studios. United Artists altered the ending a bit and added a moralistic narration by a stock actor at the beginning and end. Altman did not find out until he saw a preview of the film, and was not impressed.

## Release and legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delinquents_(1957_film)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Release and legacy")]

_The Delinquents_ received its "[gala world premiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_premiere "Film premiere")" in Kansas City in February 1957. The showing of the film was preceded by live music, a dance contest, and a parade of [Corvettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet_Corvette "Chevrolet Corvette") carrying residents who had worked on the film. It was all covered by a live radio broadcast and the theater's house lights were brought out.

The film was rejected by the [British Board of Film Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Board_of_Film_Classification "British Board of Film Classification") in 1957.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-8) United Artists released the film worldwide the next month. The film's release was not wide, and it played mostly in drive-ins. However, it did gross $1,000,000 for United Artists. When [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock") saw the film, he was apparently impressed enough to give Altman a job directing episodes of _[Alfred Hitchcock Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred\_Hitchcock\_Presents "Alfred Hitchcock Presents")_, which led to more television work for Altman over the next decade.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-9)

Rhoden produced one more film in Kansas City (_[The Cool and the Crazy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cool\_and\_the\_Crazy "The Cool and the Crazy")_) and was featured in [_TIME_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_magazine "Time magazine") as one of the "new wave" of producers. He then produced a delinquency film in Hollywood, _[Daddy-O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daddy-O\_(film) "Daddy-O (film)")_, but his mini-mogul reign was short-lived. An alcoholic who drank heavily, he died in 1959 at the age of 37 three months after suffering a heart attack.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_(1957_film)#cite_note-11)

**Stella** (or **Estela**) **Inda** (June 28, 1924 – December 7, 1995) was a Mexican [film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film "Film")[actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actress "Actress"). She was the star of notable Mexican films, including _[Los olvidados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_olvidados "Los olvidados")_ by Luis Buñuel in 1949.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stella_Inda&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Stella_Inda_en_1945.jpg/250px-Stella_Inda_en_1945.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stella_Inda_en_1945.jpg)

Stella Inda in 1945

Inda started her career as extra in the successful film _[La Mujer del Puerto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Woman\_of\_the\_Port\_(1934\_film) "The Woman of the Port (1934 film)")_ (1934), which starred [Andrea Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Palma_(actress) "Andrea Palma (actress)"). Also, she participated in Mexican films such as _[The Night of the Mayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Night\_of\_the\_Mayas "The Night of the Mayas")_ (1939), _[Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa\_(1943\_film) "Santa (1943 film)")_ (second sound version, 1943), _[Bugambilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugambilia "Bugambilia")_ (1944, with [Dolores del Río](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolores_del_R%C3%ADo "Dolores del Río")), _[Amok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amok\_(1945\_film) "Amok (1945 film)")_ (1945, with [María Félix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_F%C3%A9lix "María Félix")), and the success films _[Los olvidados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_olvidados "Los olvidados")_ (1949, directed by Luis Buñuel and _[El Rebozo de Soledad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Rebozo\_de\_Soledad "El Rebozo de Soledad")_ (1955, directed by [Roberto Gavaldón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Gavald%C3%B3n "Roberto Gavaldón")). In the later years, she was an acting teacher in the [Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_Nacional_de_Bellas_Artes "Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes") in Mexico, and directed a folkloric dance group called "Stella Inda y su Conjunto".

In 1947 she had a prominent but uncredited role as the historical personage [La Malinche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Malinche "La Malinche") in the Hollywood epic _[Captain from Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_from\_Castile "Captain from Castile")_, opposite [Cesar Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesar_Romero "Cesar Romero") as [Hernán Cortés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hern%C3%A1n_Cort%C3%A9s "Hernán Cortés").

**Stella** (or **Estela**) **Inda** (June 28, 1924 – December 7, 1995) was a Mexican [film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film "Film")[actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actress "Actress"). She was the star of notable Mexican films, including _[Los olvidados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_olvidados "Los olvidados")_ by Luis Buñuel in 1949.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stella_Inda&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Stella_Inda_en_1945.jpg/250px-Stella_Inda_en_1945.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stella_Inda_en_1945.jpg)

Stella Inda in 1945

Inda started her career as extra in the successful film _[La Mujer del Puerto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Woman\_of\_the\_Port\_(1934\_film) "The Woman of the Port (1934 film)")_ (1934), which starred [Andrea Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Palma_(actress) "Andrea Palma (actress)"). Also, she participated in Mexican films such as _[The Night of the Mayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Night\_of\_the\_Mayas "The Night of the Mayas")_ (1939), _[Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa\_(1943\_film) "Santa (1943 film)")_ (second sound version, 1943), _[Bugambilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugambilia "Bugambilia")_ (1944, with [Dolores del Río](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolores_del_R%C3%ADo "Dolores del Río")), _[Amok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amok\_(1945\_film) "Amok (1945 film)")_ (1945, with [María Félix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_F%C3%A9lix "María Félix")), and the success films _[Los olvidados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_olvidados "Los olvidados")_ (1949, directed by Luis Buñuel and _[El Rebozo de Soledad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Rebozo\_de\_Soledad "El Rebozo de Soledad")_ (1955, directed by [Roberto Gavaldón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Gavald%C3%B3n "Roberto Gavaldón")). In the later years, she was an acting teacher in the [Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_Nacional_de_Bellas_Artes "Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes") in Mexico, and directed a folkloric dance group called "Stella Inda y su Conjunto".

In 1947 she had a prominent but uncredited role as the historical personage [La Malinche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Malinche "La Malinche") in the Hollywood epic _[Captain from Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_from\_Castile "Captain from Castile")_, opposite [Cesar Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesar_Romero "Cesar Romero") as [Hernán Cortés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hern%C3%A1n_Cort%C3%A9s "Hernán Cortés").

**Richard Bakalyan** (January 29, 1931 – February 27, 2015) was an American actor who started his career playing juvenile delinquents in his first several films.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Richard Bakalyan was born on January 29, 1931, in [Watertown, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watertown,_Massachusetts "Watertown, Massachusetts"), the son of [Armenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenia "Armenia")-born William Nishan Bakalyan and Elsie Florence (née Fancy) Bakalyan, a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") from [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia"). He had two brothers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1) His father died in 1939, when Richard was 8.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-Nahigian_mirrorspectator-2)

Growing up in a tough neighborhood, Bakalyan learned [boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") to defend himself in street fights.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1) He served a year's probation at age 15 for unknown crimes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-3)

Bakalyan served in the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-ciobit-4) After four years of service, he was honorably discharged with the rank of [staff sergeant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staff_sergeant "Staff sergeant").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Film

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Film")]

Early in his career he was cast as thugs, outlaws, and in military action films, like _[The Delinquents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Delinquents\_(1957\_film) "The Delinquents (1957 film)")_ (1957), _[The Bonnie Parker Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bonnie\_Parker\_Story "The Bonnie Parker Story")_ (1958), _[Up Periscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Up\_Periscope "Up Periscope")_ (1959), and _[Panic in Year Zero!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic\_in\_Year\_Zero! "Panic in Year Zero!")_ (1962).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-5) During the filming of 1958's juvenile-gang drama _[The Cool and the Crazy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cool\_and\_the\_Crazy "The Cool and the Crazy")_, he and fellow actor Dick Jones were arrested for vagrancy while on location in [Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City "Kansas City"). They were standing on the corner between takes in "JD" outfits and the police thought that they were actual gang members. It took several hours for the film crew to explain to the police what was going on and get them released from jail.

By the mid-1960s, as he grew out of these roles, he became something of a comic heavy, often cast in family Disney films though still known in dramas. Some of his Disney projects included _[Never a Dull Moment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never\_a\_Dull\_Moment\_(1968\_film) "Never a Dull Moment (1968 film)")_ (1968), _[The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Computer\_Wore\_Tennis\_Shoes "The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes")_ (1969), _[The Strongest Man in the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Strongest\_Man\_in\_the\_World "The Strongest Man in the World")_ (1975), _[Return from Witch Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return\_from\_Witch\_Mountain "Return from Witch Mountain")_ (1978),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1) and voice-efforts in _[The Fox and the Hound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fox\_and\_the\_Hound "The Fox and the Hound")_ (1981), as 'Dinky' the finch bird.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-Nahigian_mirrorspectator-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-6)

Bakalyan had an uncredited role in _[The Greatest Story Ever Told](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Greatest\_Story\_Ever\_Told "The Greatest Story Ever Told")_ (1965) as the [good thief on the cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penitent_thief "Penitent thief"). He appeared in several of [Frank Sinatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sinatra "Frank Sinatra")'s movies during the 1960s, such as _[Robin and the 7 Hoods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin\_and\_the\_7\_Hoods "Robin and the 7 Hoods")_ (1964), _[None but the Brave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/None\_but\_the\_Brave "None but the Brave")_ (1965), and _[Von Ryan's Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von\_Ryan's\_Express "Von Ryan's Express")_ (1965), becoming lifelong friends with the Sinatra family.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-Nahigian_mirrorspectator-2) While filming _[Pressure Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure\_Point\_(1962\_film) "Pressure Point (1962 film)")_ in 1962, he met co-star [Bobby Darin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Darin "Bobby Darin"), who later became one of Bakalyan's closest friends.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-7) It's reported Bakalyan was one of the last friends to see Darin, before his premature death from heart disease, in December, 1973.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvanier2010241-8) Bakalyan played Detective Loach in [Roman Polanski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Polanski "Roman Polanski")'s 1974 film _[Chinatown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinatown\_(1974\_film) "Chinatown (1974 film)")_ opposite [Jack Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Nicholson "Jack Nicholson") and [Faye Dunaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faye_Dunaway "Faye Dunaway").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)

In 1968, Bakalyan was featured in "Way Down Cellar," a two-part story on _[Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt\_Disney\_anthology\_television\_series "Walt Disney anthology television series")_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-12) He was a regular on _Dean Martin Presents: The Bobby Darin Amusement Company_ (1972) and _The Bobby Darin Show_ (1973).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-Nahigian_mirrorspectator-2)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Bakalyan was married to Elizabeth Baumann from 1952 until her death in 1967.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-13)

A prolific character actor, Bakalyan was profiled in the book _Names You Never Remember, With Faces You Never Forget_ by Justin Humphreys.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Death")]

Bakalyan died suddenly of a [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") on February 27, 2015, at the [Arnot Ogden Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnot_Ogden_Medical_Center "Arnot Ogden Medical Center"), in [Elmira, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmira,_New_York "Elmira, New York"), aged 84.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-14)

**Richard Bakalyan** (January 29, 1931 – February 27, 2015) was an American actor who started his career playing juvenile delinquents in his first several films.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Richard Bakalyan was born on January 29, 1931, in [Watertown, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watertown,_Massachusetts "Watertown, Massachusetts"), the son of [Armenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenia "Armenia")-born William Nishan Bakalyan and Elsie Florence (née Fancy) Bakalyan, a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") from [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia"). He had two brothers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1) His father died in 1939, when Richard was 8.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-Nahigian_mirrorspectator-2)

Growing up in a tough neighborhood, Bakalyan learned [boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") to defend himself in street fights.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1) He served a year's probation at age 15 for unknown crimes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-3)

Bakalyan served in the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-ciobit-4) After four years of service, he was honorably discharged with the rank of [staff sergeant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staff_sergeant "Staff sergeant").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Film

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Film")]

Early in his career he was cast as thugs, outlaws, and in military action films, like _[The Delinquents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Delinquents\_(1957\_film) "The Delinquents (1957 film)")_ (1957), _[The Bonnie Parker Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bonnie\_Parker\_Story "The Bonnie Parker Story")_ (1958), _[Up Periscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Up\_Periscope "Up Periscope")_ (1959), and _[Panic in Year Zero!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic\_in\_Year\_Zero! "Panic in Year Zero!")_ (1962).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-5) During the filming of 1958's juvenile-gang drama _[The Cool and the Crazy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cool\_and\_the\_Crazy "The Cool and the Crazy")_, he and fellow actor Dick Jones were arrested for vagrancy while on location in [Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City "Kansas City"). They were standing on the corner between takes in "JD" outfits and the police thought that they were actual gang members. It took several hours for the film crew to explain to the police what was going on and get them released from jail.

By the mid-1960s, as he grew out of these roles, he became something of a comic heavy, often cast in family Disney films though still known in dramas. Some of his Disney projects included _[Never a Dull Moment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never\_a\_Dull\_Moment\_(1968\_film) "Never a Dull Moment (1968 film)")_ (1968), _[The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Computer\_Wore\_Tennis\_Shoes "The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes")_ (1969), _[The Strongest Man in the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Strongest\_Man\_in\_the\_World "The Strongest Man in the World")_ (1975), _[Return from Witch Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return\_from\_Witch\_Mountain "Return from Witch Mountain")_ (1978),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1) and voice-efforts in _[The Fox and the Hound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fox\_and\_the\_Hound "The Fox and the Hound")_ (1981), as 'Dinky' the finch bird.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-Nahigian_mirrorspectator-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-6)

Bakalyan had an uncredited role in _[The Greatest Story Ever Told](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Greatest\_Story\_Ever\_Told "The Greatest Story Ever Told")_ (1965) as the [good thief on the cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penitent_thief "Penitent thief"). He appeared in several of [Frank Sinatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sinatra "Frank Sinatra")'s movies during the 1960s, such as _[Robin and the 7 Hoods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin\_and\_the\_7\_Hoods "Robin and the 7 Hoods")_ (1964), _[None but the Brave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/None\_but\_the\_Brave "None but the Brave")_ (1965), and _[Von Ryan's Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von\_Ryan's\_Express "Von Ryan's Express")_ (1965), becoming lifelong friends with the Sinatra family.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-Nahigian_mirrorspectator-2) While filming _[Pressure Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure\_Point\_(1962\_film) "Pressure Point (1962 film)")_ in 1962, he met co-star [Bobby Darin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Darin "Bobby Darin"), who later became one of Bakalyan's closest friends.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-7) It's reported Bakalyan was one of the last friends to see Darin, before his premature death from heart disease, in December, 1973.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvanier2010241-8) Bakalyan played Detective Loach in [Roman Polanski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Polanski "Roman Polanski")'s 1974 film _[Chinatown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinatown\_(1974\_film) "Chinatown (1974 film)")_ opposite [Jack Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Nicholson "Jack Nicholson") and [Faye Dunaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faye_Dunaway "Faye Dunaway").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Bakalyan was married to Elizabeth Baumann from 1952 until her death in 1967.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-13)

A prolific character actor, Bakalyan was profiled in the book _Names You Never Remember, With Faces You Never Forget_ by Justin Humphreys.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHumphreys2006Dick_Bakalyan-1)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_Bakalyan&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Death")]

Bakalyan died suddenly of a [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") on February 27, 2015, at the [Arnot Ogden Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnot_Ogden_Medical_Center "Arnot Ogden Medical Center"), in [Elmira, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmira,_New_York "Elmira, New York"), aged 84.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bakalyan#cite_note-14)

**Peter Miller** (born 1968) is a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian "Canadian")[actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor "Actor").

His credits have included the television series _[MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MVP\_(TV\_series) "MVP (TV series)")_, _[Virginie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginie "Virginie")_ and _[Lance et Compte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lance\_et\_Compte "Lance et Compte")_, and the films _[Mambo Italiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo\_Italiano\_(film) "Mambo Italiano (film)")_[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-1) and _[Rouge sang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Storm\_Within\_(2013\_film) "The Storm Within (2013 film)")_. Miller portrayed [Galeazzo Maria Sforza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeazzo_Maria_Sforza "Galeazzo Maria Sforza") in the 2009 short-film series _[Assassin's Creed: Lineage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassin's\_Creed:\_Lineage "Assassin's Creed: Lineage")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-2)

Miller graduated from the [Neighborhood Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhood_Playhouse "Neighborhood Playhouse") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). He was born in [Chibougamau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chibougamau "Chibougamau"), [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") and spent part of his childhood in the [Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas "Bahamas"). His mother is of [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") descent and his father is of [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") descent. He is [anglophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language")-[francophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francophone "Francophone") bilingual.

He is also a former professional football player in the [Canadian Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Football_League "Canadian Football League"). He was drafted in the seventh round of the [1992 CFL draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_CFL_draft "1992 CFL draft") by the [Saskatchewan Roughriders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan_Roughriders "Saskatchewan Roughriders") and played six seasons in the CFL with the Roughriders, [BC Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BC_Lions "BC Lions"), and [Toronto Argonauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Argonauts "Toronto Argonauts") as a [linebacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linebacker "Linebacker"); he played [college football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football "College football") for [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Tigers_football "Pacific Tigers football").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-3)

**Peter Miller** (born 1968) is a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian "Canadian")[actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor "Actor").

His credits have included the television series _[MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MVP\_(TV\_series) "MVP (TV series)")_, _[Virginie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginie "Virginie")_ and _[Lance et Compte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lance\_et\_Compte "Lance et Compte")_, and the films _[Mambo Italiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo\_Italiano\_(film) "Mambo Italiano (film)")_[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-1) and _[Rouge sang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Storm\_Within\_(2013\_film) "The Storm Within (2013 film)")_. Miller portrayed [Galeazzo Maria Sforza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeazzo_Maria_Sforza "Galeazzo Maria Sforza") in the 2009 short-film series _[Assassin's Creed: Lineage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassin's\_Creed:\_Lineage "Assassin's Creed: Lineage")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-2)

Miller graduated from the [Neighborhood Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhood_Playhouse "Neighborhood Playhouse") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). He was born in [Chibougamau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chibougamau "Chibougamau"), [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") and spent part of his childhood in the [Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas "Bahamas"). His mother is of [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") descent and his father is of [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") descent. He is [anglophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language")-[francophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francophone "Francophone") bilingual.

He is also a former professional football player in the [Canadian Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Football_League "Canadian Football League"). He was drafted in the seventh round of the [1992 CFL draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_CFL_draft "1992 CFL draft") by the [Saskatchewan Roughriders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan_Roughriders "Saskatchewan Roughriders") and played six seasons in the CFL with the Roughriders, [BC Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BC_Lions "BC Lions"), and [Toronto Argonauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Argonauts "Toronto Argonauts") as a [linebacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linebacker "Linebacker"); he played [college football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football "College football") for [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Tigers_football "Pacific Tigers football").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-3)

_**The Brute**_ ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _**El Bruto**_) is a [1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_films_of_1953 "Mexican films of 1953")[Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico")[drama film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)") directed by Luis Buñuel and starring [Pedro Armendáriz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Armend%C3%A1riz "Pedro Armendáriz") and [Katy Jurado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katy_Jurado "Katy Jurado").

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Bruto&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Impoverished tenants are being evicted from their block of flats by their elderly landlord, Cabrera, who wants to build a house on the site for himself. The tenants refuse to leave, so the landlord, at the prompting of his young wife, Paloma, tells his strongest slaughterhouse worker, Pedro, known as El Bruto, to get rid of the ringleaders. When Pedro moves into the landlord’s house to work for him as a retail butcher and enforcer, Paloma, who also works in the shop, is strongly attracted to him. They begin an affair.

Starting the campaign, Pedro punches one of the ringleaders, the father of Meche, and kills the sick man unintentionally. This precipitates the other tenants to find and attack him, ending in a nail being stuck in his shoulder. He bursts into an apartment and, finding Meche, asks her to remove it. He falls in love with her despite her initial rejection, and faces divided loyalties as the landlord treats him like a son. El Bruto has a suspicion that the landlord had an affair with his mother when she was his maid, and is indeed his father.

When Pedro finds that Meche has been evicted and has been abandoned by the other tenants, he proposes marriage and offers her a home. When Paloma, paying another clandestine visit to Pedro, finds out that he now lives with Meche, in her jealous rage, she tells Meche that he killed her father. Meche, horrified, flees. Pedro strikes her. She returns home and tells the landlord falsely that El Bruto ravaged her. Cabrera issues instructions for Pedro to come to his house. When he does, Cabrera insults him and his mother and tries to kill him. Instead, Pedro kills him. Prompted by Paloma, the police pursue him and kill him in a shootout. The tenants are happy because they will no longer be evicted.

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Bruto&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Release")]

On 21 September 1983, the film was screened at [The Public Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Public_Theater "The Public Theater") in conjunction with the death of the director.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-1)_El Bruto_ was released on DVD on 23 October 2007.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-2) In 2023, _El Bruto_ was restored in 4K and was released on DVD by VCI Entertainment.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-3)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Bruto&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

A retrospective review praises the film, although not often mentioned by the director himself, as one of the finest of his Mexican productions.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-4)

On [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), _El Bruto_ has an approval rating of 88% based on 8 reviews, with an average score of 7.5/10.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-5)

## Accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Bruto&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Accolades")]

Andrés Soler was nominated for the [Ariel Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Award "Ariel Award") in the Best Supporting Actor category for _The Brute_, while [Katy Jurado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katy_Jurado "Katy Jurado") won in the Best Supporting Actress category. The film also was nominated for the Ariel Award in the Best Cinematography category in 1954.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

_**The Brute**_ ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _**El Bruto**_) is a [1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_films_of_1953 "Mexican films of 1953")[Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico")[drama film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)") directed by Luis Buñuel and starring [Pedro Armendáriz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Armend%C3%A1riz "Pedro Armendáriz") and [Katy Jurado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katy_Jurado "Katy Jurado").

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Bruto&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Impoverished tenants are being evicted from their block of flats by their elderly landlord, Cabrera, who wants to build a house on the site for himself. The tenants refuse to leave, so the landlord, at the prompting of his young wife, Paloma, tells his strongest slaughterhouse worker, Pedro, known as El Bruto, to get rid of the ringleaders. When Pedro moves into the landlord’s house to work for him as a retail butcher and enforcer, Paloma, who also works in the shop, is strongly attracted to him. They begin an affair.

Starting the campaign, Pedro punches one of the ringleaders, the father of Meche, and kills the sick man unintentionally. This precipitates the other tenants to find and attack him, ending in a nail being stuck in his shoulder. He bursts into an apartment and, finding Meche, asks her to remove it. He falls in love with her despite her initial rejection, and faces divided loyalties as the landlord treats him like a son. El Bruto has a suspicion that the landlord had an affair with his mother when she was his maid, and is indeed his father.

When Pedro finds that Meche has been evicted and has been abandoned by the other tenants, he proposes marriage and offers her a home. When Paloma, paying another clandestine visit to Pedro, finds out that he now lives with Meche, in her jealous rage, she tells Meche that he killed her father. Meche, horrified, flees. Pedro strikes her. She returns home and tells the landlord falsely that El Bruto ravaged her. Cabrera issues instructions for Pedro to come to his house. When he does, Cabrera insults him and his mother and tries to kill him. Instead, Pedro kills him. Prompted by Paloma, the police pursue him and kill him in a shootout. The tenants are happy because they will no longer be evicted.

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Bruto&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Release")]

On 21 September 1983, the film was screened at [The Public Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Public_Theater "The Public Theater") in conjunction with the death of the director.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-1)_El Bruto_ was released on DVD on 23 October 2007.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-2) In 2023, _El Bruto_ was restored in 4K and was released on DVD by VCI Entertainment.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-3)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Bruto&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

A retrospective review praises the film, although not often mentioned by the director himself, as one of the finest of his Mexican productions.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-4)

On [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), _El Bruto_ has an approval rating of 88% based on 8 reviews, with an average score of 7.5/10.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bruto#cite_note-5)

## Accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Bruto&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Accolades")]

Andrés Soler was nominated for the [Ariel Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Award "Ariel Award") in the Best Supporting Actor category for _The Brute_, while [Katy Jurado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katy_Jurado "Katy Jurado") won in the Best Supporting Actress category. The film also was nominated for the Ariel Award in the Best Cinematography category in 1954.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

_**Él**_,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-com-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-cah-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-mex-4) (also [stylized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylized_name "Stylized name")_**El**_ and _**EL**_,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-can-8)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-cah-3)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-BOM-1) and released in the US[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] as _**This Strange Passion**_[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-com-2)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-rot-9)) is a 1953[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-com-2) Mexican film by Luis Buñuel based upon [the novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89l_(novel) "Él (novel)") by [Mercedes Pinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_Pinto "Mercedes Pinto"). The film explores several of Buñuel’s signature cinematic themes, most notably a romance warped by a bourgeois husband's obsessive paranoia, interspersed with distinct surrealist touches.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-10)[_[improper synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research#Synthesis\_of\_published\_material "Wikipedia:No original research")_] The film was entered into the [1953 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Cannes_Film_Festival "1953 Cannes Film Festival").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-can-8)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%C3%89l_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

The film opens on [Good Friday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Friday "Good Friday") during a traditional [foot-washing ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maundy_(foot_washing) "Maundy (foot washing)"). Francisco, an affluent and seemingly upstanding conservative, is instantly captivated by a beautiful young woman named Gloria. Consumed by a sudden obsession, he spends subsequent mornings searching for her in the same church. When he finally corners her, Gloria insists they cannot speak, but Francisco undeterred, tracks her to a restaurant. There, he discovers she is meeting Raúl—a close friend of his.

When Raúl casually reveals that he and Gloria are engaged, Francisco secretly plots to steal her away. He orchestrates an elegant party to flaunt his high social standing and charm. Though Gloria is initially wary of his sudden intrusion into her life, she ultimately succumbs to his sophisticated veneer and accepts his courtship.

The narrative then shifts to the future. Raúl, driving through the city, accidentally crosses paths with a visibly distressed Gloria. As she opens up to him, the film transitions into an extended flashback detailing the horrific reality of her marriage.

Behind closed doors, Francisco is a man consumed by intense paranoia and pathological jealousy. Compounding his mental instability, Francisco is locked in a stressful property lawsuit that heightens his agitation. Meanwhile, despite her total innocence, Gloria is entirely isolated. Her mother refuses to believe such a respected community figure could be abusive and Father Velasco, admonishes Gloria for her "untoward" behavior, vouching for Francisco’s purity. When Francisco discovers Gloria confided in the priest, he subjects her to a terrifying mock execution, shooting her with a revolver loaded with blanks to "teach her a lesson." This burst of violence is then followed by a temporary period of warmth and remorse. The peace is short-lived. During a trip to a church bell tower, Francisco’s facade slips entirely. Looking down at the street, he launches into a misanthropic tirade and turns his rage abruptly on Gloria. He apparently attempts to strangle her, threatening to hurl her over the railing. Gloria narrowly escapes—bringing the flashback full circle to her chance encounter with Raúl.

Raúl urges her to leave him, but when Gloria returns home to pack, Francisco discovers Raúl dropped her off. The cycle of jealousy reignites. Though he briefly seeks reconciliation after realizing she never had a physical affair, his fury returns when Gloria admits she confided their marital problems to Raúl.

That night, Francisco’s psychosis reaches a breaking point as he attempts to bind and mutilate Gloria in her sleep. Her screams startle him, causing him to retreat to his room in a broken, weeping heap as he realizes he is losing control of his actions. By morning, Gloria has fled for good. Armed with his revolver, Francisco frantically hunts for her. Spotting what he believes to be Gloria and Raúl in a car, he pursues them back to the very church where he first saw her. Inside, he realizes the couple is actually a pair of strangers.

Plunging into total madness, Francisco hallucinates that the entire congregation—including the priest—is mocking him. He charges the altar in a manic frenzy and attacks the priest. Even as the congregation subdues him, the priest pities him, shouting, "Don't hurt him, he's my friend; he's gone mad!"

Years later, Gloria and Raúl visit a peaceful monastery with their young son. It is revealed that the monks have taken Francisco in. Gloria and Raúl choose to avoid him, but it is revealed that they have named their son Francisco. After they leave, the head monk informs Francisco of their visit. Francisco calmly notes that the boy is clearly Raúl and Gloria's, quietly murmuring, "Time has proven my point." "But to what avail?" The film closes on Francisco wandering down a monastery path and disappearing into a dark doorway.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%C3%89l_(film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

After completing the initial filming of _[Adventures of Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventures\_of\_Robinson\_Crusoe "Adventures of Robinson Crusoe")_ and its release being indefinitely delayed, Buñuel decided to adapt Mercedes Pinto's novel _Pensamientos_ about a paranoid husband. Buñuel also added personal memories of his sister Conchita's paranoid husband,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):227 who once mistakenly thought he saw Buñuel making vulgar faces at him on the street and went home to get his gun until his family finally convinced him that Buñuel was living in Zaragoza at the time. Buñuel acknowledged autobiographical elements in the film and stated that "it may be the film I put the most of myself into. There is something of me in the protagonist."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):228

Buñuel later complained about how fast he was forced to shoot the film and that he wanted to remake it. He stated that "I did what I did in most of my Mexican films. They proposed a subject to me and instead of it, I made a counter-offer which, though still commercial, seemed more propitious for examining the things that interested me."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):228 Buñuel's producer hired Yucatán-born Mexican actor [Arturo de Córdova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_de_C%C3%B3rdova "Arturo de Córdova") for the lead role of Francisco Galvan de Montemayor. De Córdova had previously been a Hollywood star in swashbuckling roles, but his heavy Bronx accent often hindered his performances. Buñuel playfully has a cameo in the film's last scene as a priest.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):228

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%C3%89l_(film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

_Él_ was a critical and financial disappointment, and many audience members in Mexico laughed during the film. Buñuel later stated that he was disappointed by the film overall, but proud that French psychoanalyst [Jacques Lacan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Lacan "Jacques Lacan") was known to screen the film for his students as an example of paranoia.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):228

In recent years, the reputation of _Él_ has considerably increased; the film holds a [100% approval rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_with_a_100%25_rating_on_Rotten_Tomatoes "List of films with a 100% rating on Rotten Tomatoes") on Rotten Tomatoes,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-rot-9) and the French magazine _[Cahiers du Cinéma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahiers\_du\_Cin%C3%A9ma "Cahiers du Cinéma")_ named it one of the 100 essential films of all time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-cah-3)

The film was ranked number 7 in the list of the Best 100 Mexican films of all time according to 25 cinema critics (1994/2020).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-mex-4)
