_**Él**_,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-com-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-cah-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-mex-4) (also [stylized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylized_name "Stylized name")_**El**_ and _**EL**_,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-can-8)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-cah-3)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-BOM-1) and released in the US[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] as _**This Strange Passion**_[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-com-2)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-rot-9)) is a 1953[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-com-2) Mexican film by Luis Buñuel based upon [the novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89l_(novel) "Él (novel)") by [Mercedes Pinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_Pinto "Mercedes Pinto"). The film explores several of Buñuel’s signature cinematic themes, most notably a romance warped by a bourgeois husband's obsessive paranoia, interspersed with distinct surrealist touches.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-10)[_[improper synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research#Synthesis\_of\_published\_material "Wikipedia:No original research")_] The film was entered into the [1953 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Cannes_Film_Festival "1953 Cannes Film Festival").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-can-8)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%C3%89l_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

The film opens on [Good Friday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Friday "Good Friday") during a traditional [foot-washing ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maundy_(foot_washing) "Maundy (foot washing)"). Francisco, an affluent and seemingly upstanding conservative, is instantly captivated by a beautiful young woman named Gloria. Consumed by a sudden obsession, he spends subsequent mornings searching for her in the same church. When he finally corners her, Gloria insists they cannot speak, but Francisco undeterred, tracks her to a restaurant. There, he discovers she is meeting Raúl—a close friend of his.

When Raúl casually reveals that he and Gloria are engaged, Francisco secretly plots to steal her away. He orchestrates an elegant party to flaunt his high social standing and charm. Though Gloria is initially wary of his sudden intrusion into her life, she ultimately succumbs to his sophisticated veneer and accepts his courtship.

The narrative then shifts to the future. Raúl, driving through the city, accidentally crosses paths with a visibly distressed Gloria. As she opens up to him, the film transitions into an extended flashback detailing the horrific reality of her marriage.

Behind closed doors, Francisco is a man consumed by intense paranoia and pathological jealousy. Compounding his mental instability, Francisco is locked in a stressful property lawsuit that heightens his agitation. Meanwhile, despite her total innocence, Gloria is entirely isolated. Her mother refuses to believe such a respected community figure could be abusive and Father Velasco, admonishes Gloria for her "untoward" behavior, vouching for Francisco’s purity. When Francisco discovers Gloria confided in the priest, he subjects her to a terrifying mock execution, shooting her with a revolver loaded with blanks to "teach her a lesson." This burst of violence is then followed by a temporary period of warmth and remorse. The peace is short-lived. During a trip to a church bell tower, Francisco’s facade slips entirely. Looking down at the street, he launches into a misanthropic tirade and turns his rage abruptly on Gloria. He apparently attempts to strangle her, threatening to hurl her over the railing. Gloria narrowly escapes—bringing the flashback full circle to her chance encounter with Raúl.

Raúl urges her to leave him, but when Gloria returns home to pack, Francisco discovers Raúl dropped her off. The cycle of jealousy reignites. Though he briefly seeks reconciliation after realizing she never had a physical affair, his fury returns when Gloria admits she confided their marital problems to Raúl.

That night, Francisco’s psychosis reaches a breaking point as he attempts to bind and mutilate Gloria in her sleep. Her screams startle him, causing him to retreat to his room in a broken, weeping heap as he realizes he is losing control of his actions. By morning, Gloria has fled for good. Armed with his revolver, Francisco frantically hunts for her. Spotting what he believes to be Gloria and Raúl in a car, he pursues them back to the very church where he first saw her. Inside, he realizes the couple is actually a pair of strangers.

Plunging into total madness, Francisco hallucinates that the entire congregation—including the priest—is mocking him. He charges the altar in a manic frenzy and attacks the priest. Even as the congregation subdues him, the priest pities him, shouting, "Don't hurt him, he's my friend; he's gone mad!"

Years later, Gloria and Raúl visit a peaceful monastery with their young son. It is revealed that the monks have taken Francisco in. Gloria and Raúl choose to avoid him, but it is revealed that they have named their son Francisco. After they leave, the head monk informs Francisco of their visit. Francisco calmly notes that the boy is clearly Raúl and Gloria's, quietly murmuring, "Time has proven my point." "But to what avail?" The film closes on Francisco wandering down a monastery path and disappearing into a dark doorway.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%C3%89l_(film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

After completing the initial filming of _[Adventures of Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventures\_of\_Robinson\_Crusoe "Adventures of Robinson Crusoe")_ and its release being indefinitely delayed, Buñuel decided to adapt Mercedes Pinto's novel _Pensamientos_ about a paranoid husband. Buñuel also added personal memories of his sister Conchita's paranoid husband,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):227 who once mistakenly thought he saw Buñuel making vulgar faces at him on the street and went home to get his gun until his family finally convinced him that Buñuel was living in Zaragoza at the time. Buñuel acknowledged autobiographical elements in the film and stated that "it may be the film I put the most of myself into. There is something of me in the protagonist."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):228

Buñuel later complained about how fast he was forced to shoot the film and that he wanted to remake it. He stated that "I did what I did in most of my Mexican films. They proposed a subject to me and instead of it, I made a counter-offer which, though still commercial, seemed more propitious for examining the things that interested me."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):228 Buñuel's producer hired Yucatán-born Mexican actor [Arturo de Córdova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_de_C%C3%B3rdova "Arturo de Córdova") for the lead role of Francisco Galvan de Montemayor. De Córdova had previously been a Hollywood star in swashbuckling roles, but his heavy Bronx accent often hindered his performances. Buñuel playfully has a cameo in the film's last scene as a priest.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):228

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%C3%89l_(film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

_Él_ was a critical and financial disappointment, and many audience members in Mexico laughed during the film. Buñuel later stated that he was disappointed by the film overall, but proud that French psychoanalyst [Jacques Lacan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Lacan "Jacques Lacan") was known to screen the film for his students as an example of paranoia.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-bax-11):228

In recent years, the reputation of _Él_ has considerably increased; the film holds a [100% approval rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_with_a_100%25_rating_on_Rotten_Tomatoes "List of films with a 100% rating on Rotten Tomatoes") on Rotten Tomatoes,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-rot-9) and the French magazine _[Cahiers du Cinéma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahiers\_du\_Cin%C3%A9ma "Cahiers du Cinéma")_ named it one of the 100 essential films of all time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-cah-3)

The film was ranked number 7 in the list of the Best 100 Mexican films of all time according to 25 cinema critics (1994/2020).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(film)#cite_note-mex-4)

_**The Lovers**_ ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Les amants_) is a 1958 French [drama film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)") directed by Louis Malle which stars [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau"), [Alain Cuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alain_Cuny "Alain Cuny"), and [Jean-Marc Bory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Marc_Bory "Jean-Marc Bory"). Based on the posthumously-published 1876 short story "Point de Lendemain" ("No Tomorrow") by [Dominique Vivant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Vivant "Dominique Vivant") (1747–1825), the film concerns a woman involved in adultery who rediscovers human love. _The Lovers_ was Malle's second feature film, made when he was 25 years old. The film was a box-office hit in France when released theatrically, gaining 2,594,160 admissions in France alone. The film was highly controversial when released in the United States for its depiction of allegedly obscene material. At the 1958 [Venice Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Film_Festival "Venice Film Festival"), the film won the [Grand Jury Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Jury_Prize_(Venice_Film_Festival) "Grand Jury Prize (Venice Film Festival)") and was nominated for the [Golden Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion").

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Lovers_(1958_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Jeanne Tournier ([Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau")) lives with her husband Henri ([Alain Cuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alain_Cuny "Alain Cuny")) and young daughter, Catherine, in a mansion near [Dijon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijon "Dijon"). Her emotionally remote husband is a busy newspaper owner who has little time for his wife, except when he chooses to place demands upon her; often they sleep in separate rooms. Jeanne escapes to Paris regularly where she can spend time with her chic friend Maggy ([Judith Magre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Magre "Judith Magre")) and the polo-playing Raoul ([José Luis de Vilallonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Luis_de_Vilallonga "José Luis de Vilallonga")), Maggy's friend and Jeanne's lover.

Jeanne's constant talk of her two friends leads to Henri demanding that she invite them to dinner and to stay as overnight guests. Jeanne's car, however, breaks down on the day of the dinner party. Because of this, she accepts a lift from a younger man named Bernard ([Jean-Marc Bory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Marc_Bory "Jean-Marc Bory")) and then asks him to drive her home. By the time they get back, Maggy and Raoul have already arrived at the mansion. It transpires that Bernard, an archaeologist, is the son of a friend of Jeanne's husband, and he too is added to the guest list. Jeanne spurns Raoul's advances, claiming that it is too dangerous.

Late at night, Jeanne pours herself a drink and, wearing her nightgown, walks on the gardens outside the mansion. There, she stumbles upon Bernard, who is smitten with her. At first, she wants him to leave her alone, but the two eventually start connecting. The two kiss and end up spending time in a small boat on a nearby river. They then sneak back into the mansion, where he learns of Catherine's existence and later has sex with Jeanne. In the morning, to the surprise of everyone, Jeanne leaves with Bernard, planning to never return. Initially, she has doubts, but ends up committing to spending the rest of her life with him.

## Critical reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Lovers_(1958_film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Critical reception")]

[John Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Simon_(critic) "John Simon (critic)") described _The Lovers_ as "undistinguished but sexy".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lovers_(1958_film)#cite_note-3)

Critic Pauline Kael wrote that the film was "facile movie-poetry but erotic and beautifully made."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lovers_(1958_film)#cite_note-4)

## American obscenity case

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Lovers_(1958_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: American obscenity case")]

Main article: [Jacobellis v. Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobellis_v._Ohio "Jacobellis v. Ohio")

The film is important in American legal history as it resulted in a court case that questioned the definition of obscenity. A showing of the film at [Coventry Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_Village "Coventry Village") in [Cleveland Heights, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Heights,_Ohio "Cleveland Heights, Ohio") resulted in a criminal conviction of the theatre manager for public depiction of [obscene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obscene "Obscene") material. He appealed his conviction to the [United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States"), which reversed the conviction and ruled that the film was not obscene in its written opinion (_[Jacobellis v. Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobellis\_v.\_Ohio "Jacobellis v. Ohio")_). The case resulted in Justice [Potter Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potter_Stewart "Potter Stewart")'s famously subjective definition of hard-core pornography: "[I know it when I see it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_know_it_when_I_see_it "I know it when I see it")." (Stewart did not consider the film to be such.)

_**The Lovers**_ ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Les amants_) is a 1958 French [drama film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)") directed by Louis Malle which stars [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau"), [Alain Cuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alain_Cuny "Alain Cuny"), and [Jean-Marc Bory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Marc_Bory "Jean-Marc Bory"). Based on the posthumously-published 1876 short story "Point de Lendemain" ("No Tomorrow") by [Dominique Vivant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Vivant "Dominique Vivant") (1747–1825), the film concerns a woman involved in adultery who rediscovers human love. _The Lovers_ was Malle's second feature film, made when he was 25 years old. The film was a box-office hit in France when released theatrically, gaining 2,594,160 admissions in France alone. The film was highly controversial when released in the United States for its depiction of allegedly obscene material. At the 1958 [Venice Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Film_Festival "Venice Film Festival"), the film won the [Grand Jury Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Jury_Prize_(Venice_Film_Festival) "Grand Jury Prize (Venice Film Festival)") and was nominated for the [Golden Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion").

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Lovers_(1958_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Jeanne Tournier ([Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau")) lives with her husband Henri ([Alain Cuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alain_Cuny "Alain Cuny")) and young daughter, Catherine, in a mansion near [Dijon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijon "Dijon"). Her emotionally remote husband is a busy newspaper owner who has little time for his wife, except when he chooses to place demands upon her; often they sleep in separate rooms. Jeanne escapes to Paris regularly where she can spend time with her chic friend Maggy ([Judith Magre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Magre "Judith Magre")) and the polo-playing Raoul ([José Luis de Vilallonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Luis_de_Vilallonga "José Luis de Vilallonga")), Maggy's friend and Jeanne's lover.

Jeanne's constant talk of her two friends leads to Henri demanding that she invite them to dinner and to stay as overnight guests. Jeanne's car, however, breaks down on the day of the dinner party. Because of this, she accepts a lift from a younger man named Bernard ([Jean-Marc Bory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Marc_Bory "Jean-Marc Bory")) and then asks him to drive her home. By the time they get back, Maggy and Raoul have already arrived at the mansion. It transpires that Bernard, an archaeologist, is the son of a friend of Jeanne's husband, and he too is added to the guest list. Jeanne spurns Raoul's advances, claiming that it is too dangerous.

Late at night, Jeanne pours herself a drink and, wearing her nightgown, walks on the gardens outside the mansion. There, she stumbles upon Bernard, who is smitten with her. At first, she wants him to leave her alone, but the two eventually start connecting. The two kiss and end up spending time in a small boat on a nearby river. They then sneak back into the mansion, where he learns of Catherine's existence and later has sex with Jeanne. In the morning, to the surprise of everyone, Jeanne leaves with Bernard, planning to never return. Initially, she has doubts, but ends up committing to spending the rest of her life with him.

## American obscenity case

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Lovers_(1958_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: American obscenity case")]

Main article: [Jacobellis v. Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobellis_v._Ohio "Jacobellis v. Ohio")

The film is important in American legal history as it resulted in a court case that questioned the definition of obscenity. A showing of the film at [Coventry Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_Village "Coventry Village") in [Cleveland Heights, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Heights,_Ohio "Cleveland Heights, Ohio") resulted in a criminal conviction of the theatre manager for public depiction of [obscene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obscene "Obscene") material. He appealed his conviction to the [United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States"), which reversed the conviction and ruled that the film was not obscene in its written opinion (_[Jacobellis v. Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobellis\_v.\_Ohio "Jacobellis v. Ohio")_). The case resulted in Justice [Potter Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potter_Stewart "Potter Stewart")'s famously subjective definition of hard-core pornography: "[I know it when I see it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_know_it_when_I_see_it "I know it when I see it")." (Stewart did not consider the film to be such.)

_**Elevator to the Gallows**_[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-1) (French: _**Ascenseur pour l'échafaud**_) is a 1958 French [crime thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_thriller_film "Crime thriller film")[tragedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy "Tragedy") film directed by Louis Malle in his directorial debut. The film stars [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau") and [Maurice Ronet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ronet "Maurice Ronet") as lovers whose murder plot starts to unravel after one of them becomes trapped in an elevator. The screenplay by [Roger Nimier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Nimier "Roger Nimier") and Malle is based on the 1956 novel of the same name by Noël Calef.

Associated by some critics with [film noir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_noir "Film noir")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-2) and introducing new narrative, cinematographic, and editing techniques, the film is considered an important work in establishing the [French New Wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_New_Wave "French New Wave") and the [New Modern Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_art_cinema "European art cinema").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-romina-3) The [improvised soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascenseur_pour_l'%C3%A9chafaud_(soundtrack) "Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (soundtrack)") by [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") and the relationship the film establishes among music, image, and emotion were considered groundbreaking.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Lovers Florence Carala and Julien Tavernier devise a plan to kill Florence's husband Simon, a wealthy French industrialist who is also Julien's boss. Staying late at the office one Saturday, Julien, an ex-[Foreign Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Foreign_Legion "French Foreign Legion") parachutist and veteran of the [Indochinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Indochina_War "First Indochina War") and [Algerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algerian_War "Algerian War") wars, climbs the side of the building to Simon's office and kills him with his own gun, then stages the body as a suicide. He leaves the building with a secretary and security guard to provide alibis. He glances up from his car and realizes he left his climbing rope hanging from the balcony rail. Leaving the engine running, he rushes back into the building and boards the elevator just before the security guard switches off the power and locks up for the weekend, trapping Julien between floors.

Louis, a young small-time crook, and his girlfriend Véronique, a flower shop assistant, steal Julien's running car and drive past Florence, who is waiting for Julien at a nearby café. The sight of Véronique convinces her Julien abandoned their plan and picked up another girl and she wanders the streets despondently searching for him in local nightclubs.

Louis and Véronique drive around for hours, until some Germans in a [sporty Mercedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_300_SL "Mercedes-Benz 300 SL") challenge Louis to a race. He follows them to a motel, and the German driver, the jovial Horst Bencker, invites Louis and Véronique to have a drink with him and his wife Frieda. Both couples check in and, while they chat, Frieda takes a few pictures of Louis and her husband with Julien's camera. She finishes the roll, so Véronique drops the film off at the motel's photo lab.

After the Benckers go to bed, Louis is caught by Horst attempting to steal the Mercedes, and Louis empties Julien's pistol into them. He and Véronique return to Véronique's apartment in Paris and Véronique persuades Louis to attempt suicide with her by taking [phenobarbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenobarbital "Phenobarbital") pills.

The police discover the French couple at the hotel registered as "Mr. and Mrs. Julien Tavernier" and find Julien's car and gun next to the Benckers' corpses and Julien's raincoat in their stolen Mercedes. They search Julien's office, escorted by the security guard, and discover Simon's body. Once the building's power is switched back on, Julien escapes from the elevator and goes to a cafe, unaware that he has been identified as a murder suspect in the morning newspapers. He is arrested and charged with the murder of the Benckers, unable to convince the police that he was trapped in the elevator all weekend. The rope he left attached to the balcony eventually falls loose on its own.

Florence obtains Véronique's address from the florist and finds Véronique and Louis still alive. She accuses the drowsy couple of murdering the Benckers and calls the police with an anonymous tip. Louis believes he's gotten away with the murder when he sees Julien's picture in the paper, but Véronique reminds him of the roll of film. Louis rushes to the motel's photo lab, tailed by Florence, and is arrested on the spot. Inside the lab Commissaire Cherrier shows Florence the photos of her and Julien that have been developed and are now evidence against them. Cherrier informs Florence she will probably get a harsher sentence than Julien, and Florence replies she did it for love and believes she will one day be reunited with Julien.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

This low-budget black-and-white production was 24-year-old Louis Malle's first feature film. He had previously worked with [Jacques Cousteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Cousteau "Jacques Cousteau") for several years, and was credited as co-director of the documentary _[The Silent World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silent\_World "The Silent World")_ (1956).

Malle cast [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau") after seeing her in the Paris stage production of [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams")' _[Cat on a Hot Tin Roof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat\_on\_a\_Hot\_Tin\_Roof "Cat on a Hot Tin Roof")_. She had already been in a number of films, but her role in this film is often considered her breakthrough. Malle filmed her without the heavy makeup and extreme lighting that previous directors had demanded. Scenes of Moreau wandering down the [Champs Elysees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champs_Elysees "Champs Elysees") at night were shot on fast film from a baby carriage using only available light from the street and shop windows.

## Soundtrack

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Soundtrack")]

Main article: [Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (soundtrack)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascenseur_pour_l'%C3%A9chafaud_(soundtrack) "Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (soundtrack)")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg)

Jazz trumpeter [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), who produced an innovative score for _Elevator to the Gallows_, pictured in 1956.

[Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s score for the film is considered by many to be groundbreaking,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-romina-3) with jazz critic Phil Johnson describing it as "the loneliest trumpet sound you will ever hear, and the model for sad-core music ever since. Hear it and weep."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-4)[Richard Brody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Brody "Richard Brody"), film critic and writer for _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_, wrote in 2016 that the score itself is "better than the film, by far".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

### Recording

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recording")]

In 1957, Davis, an already well known and highly regarded jazz performer and composer, received an invitation to perform in a three-week tour of Europe as a solo artist. Davis had just abandoned his "[first great quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#First_Great_Quintet/Sextet_(1955%E2%80%9358) "Miles Davis Quintet")" of 1955–56, including saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), due to their addiction to heroin. He was beginning to try and live a healthier life, although he was still using cocaine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989209-6) Additionally, Davis, during his time performing, had been experiencing an immense amount of racism and enjoyed the chance to leave the United States for a while.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7)

Marcel Romano, promoter and jazz enthusiast, picked Davis up from the airport in November 1957 with the initial intention of telling him he would feature in a film about jazz.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7) However, this plan fell through before Davis even arrived. Instead, film technician Jean-Claude Rappeneau, whom Romano had hired for the project, mentioned that he had been working on a feature film with young director Louis Malle who had an interest in jazz music.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7) Romano told Davis about the film and said Davis seemed interested in the project, so they organised a private screening for him. Davis took notes, asking questions about the relationships between the characters and explanations of the plot. He later wrote in his autobiography that he agreed to the job because he had never written music for a film before and it would be "a great learning experience".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989217-8)

While touring Europe, Davis asked that a piano be brought to his hotel room. Over the next two weeks, he began to improvise some themes that would be used in the film.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5) Davis chose to use musicians he had been performing with on his European tour: saxophonist [Barney Wilen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barney_Wilen "Barney Wilen"), pianist [René Urtreger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Urtreger "René Urtreger"), bassist [Pierre Michelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Michelot "Pierre Michelot") and drummer [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke"). They had only been informed about the project a couple of days prior and went into the session unprepared, having not even seen the film.

On 4 December 1957 at 10 p.m., Davis and his band went to the Le Poste Parisien studios to record the score. The band drank together for an hour, played for four hours, then took two hours of editing, and left the studio by 5 a.m. the next day having finished the film score.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-9)

### Analysis and influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Analysis and influence")]

The soundtrack features eight of Davis's extended improvisations, all recorded in the four-hour session. The only song mapped out in detail was "Sur L'Autoroute", and Davis gave minimal instructions to the band for the rest of the soundtrack. He gave them two chordal structures, D minor and C seventh chords, and they improvised around these.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-Allmusic-10) Scales rather than chords took precedence, maintaining harmonic simplicity and fragmenting the themes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7) Michelot said in a 1988 interview, "What characterised the session is the absence of a defined theme."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

The mood of the soundtrack is described as generally "dour and somber",[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-Allmusic-10) but the pace is picked up on tracks such as "Dîner au Motel". The songs "Générique" and "L'Assassinat de Carala" feature Davis's distinctive trumpet style that is echoed through dire straits or death wish motifs.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-Allmusic-10) Phil Johnson further described the soundtrack as a "powerfully expressive, highly concentrated, freely inspired performance".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

The scoring process for _Elevator to the Gallows_ was a milestone event in the development of Davis's theory of [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5) Modal jazz became highly influential in the late '50s and '60s, switching from the chorally dense sound of [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"). Davis opened up a new gateway between composition and improvisation in this soundtrack, a pathway which he would explore in the 1959 modal jazz album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind\_of\_Blue "Kind of Blue")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7) This style of music would influence not only future jazz musicians but the sound of film noir itself. Richard Brody highlights this in his article, writing, "The use of jazz and jazz-derived soundtracks became so predominant, that jazz came to seem like the natural backdrop for high-speed chases, mass mayhem, and cold-blooded murder, because the films for which jazz players were enlisted were uniformly violent."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

## Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Critical response")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Identite-LouisMalle-1958-Sacem.png/250px-Identite-LouisMalle-1958-Sacem.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Identite-LouisMalle-1958-Sacem.png)

Malle in 1958

For _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_, journalist [Barry Farrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Farrell_(journalist) "Barry Farrell (journalist)") wrote:

> Moreau had 20 forgettable films behind her. ... Malle put Moreau under an honest light and wisely let his camera linger. The film was nothing special, but it did accomplish one thing: it proposed a new ideal of cinematic realism, a new way to look at a woman. All the drama in the story was in Moreau's face—the face that had been hidden behind cosmetics and flattering lights in all her earlier films. When Malle [made] _[The Lovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lovers\_(1958\_film) "The Lovers (1958 film)")_ the following year, it was obvious who his woman would be. For one thing, he had discovered her, and for another, they were in love.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-11)

In a review of the film's 2005 theatrical re-release, [Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") observed that Moreau's face when Florence is pondering Julien's whereabouts "is often illuminated only by the lights of the cafes and shops that she passes; at a time when actresses were lit and photographed with care, these scenes had a shock value, and influenced many films to come." He further argued that Louis and Véronique were a precursor to the young couple in [Jean-Luc Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Godard "Jean-Luc Godard")'s _[Breathless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathless\_(1960\_film) "Breathless (1960 film)")_ (1960).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-12) In a 2016 article, _[New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_ film critic [Richard Brody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Brody "Richard Brody") claimed the film is more important for its place in French film history than for its own artistic merits, with the exception of Davis's score, which he said "is worth hearing entirely on its own. It's better than the film itself, by far, and there are better ways to hear it than in the movie—namely, by listening to a CD that features the entire studio sessions from which the score was edited."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film holds an approval rating of 93% based on 60 reviews, with an average rating of 8.30/10. The website's critics consensus reads, "Louis Malle's hypnotic debut is a noir with genuine soul, infusing its tale of best laid plans gone awry with wistful performances, swooning cinematography, and a sultry soundtrack."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-13)[Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 94 out of 100, based on 16 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-14)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Remakes")]

There have been two film adaptations of Calef's novel since Malle's version: _Shikeidai No Erebêtâ_ (2010), by Japanese filmmaker [Akira Ogata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akira_Ogata_(film_director) "Akira Ogata (film director)"), and _Weekend_ (2013), by Russian filmmaker [Stanislav Govorukhin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanislav_Govorukhin "Stanislav Govorukhin").

_**Elevator to the Gallows**_[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-1) (French: _**Ascenseur pour l'échafaud**_) is a 1958 French [crime thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_thriller_film "Crime thriller film")[tragedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy "Tragedy") film directed by Louis Malle in his directorial debut. The film stars [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau") and [Maurice Ronet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ronet "Maurice Ronet") as lovers whose murder plot starts to unravel after one of them becomes trapped in an elevator. The screenplay by [Roger Nimier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Nimier "Roger Nimier") and Malle is based on the 1956 novel of the same name by Noël Calef.

Associated by some critics with [film noir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_noir "Film noir")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-2) and introducing new narrative, cinematographic, and editing techniques, the film is considered an important work in establishing the [French New Wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_New_Wave "French New Wave") and the [New Modern Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_art_cinema "European art cinema").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-romina-3) The [improvised soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascenseur_pour_l'%C3%A9chafaud_(soundtrack) "Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (soundtrack)") by [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") and the relationship the film establishes among music, image, and emotion were considered groundbreaking.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Lovers Florence Carala and Julien Tavernier devise a plan to kill Florence's husband Simon, a wealthy French industrialist who is also Julien's boss. Staying late at the office one Saturday, Julien, an ex-[Foreign Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Foreign_Legion "French Foreign Legion") parachutist and veteran of the [Indochinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Indochina_War "First Indochina War") and [Algerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algerian_War "Algerian War") wars, climbs the side of the building to Simon's office and kills him with his own gun, then stages the body as a suicide. He leaves the building with a secretary and security guard to provide alibis. He glances up from his car and realizes he left his climbing rope hanging from the balcony rail. Leaving the engine running, he rushes back into the building and boards the elevator just before the security guard switches off the power and locks up for the weekend, trapping Julien between floors.

Louis, a young small-time crook, and his girlfriend Véronique, a flower shop assistant, steal Julien's running car and drive past Florence, who is waiting for Julien at a nearby café. The sight of Véronique convinces her Julien abandoned their plan and picked up another girl and she wanders the streets despondently searching for him in local nightclubs.

Louis and Véronique drive around for hours, until some Germans in a [sporty Mercedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_300_SL "Mercedes-Benz 300 SL") challenge Louis to a race. He follows them to a motel, and the German driver, the jovial Horst Bencker, invites Louis and Véronique to have a drink with him and his wife Frieda. Both couples check in and, while they chat, Frieda takes a few pictures of Louis and her husband with Julien's camera. She finishes the roll, so Véronique drops the film off at the motel's photo lab.

After the Benckers go to bed, Louis is caught by Horst attempting to steal the Mercedes, and Louis empties Julien's pistol into them. He and Véronique return to Véronique's apartment in Paris and Véronique persuades Louis to attempt suicide with her by taking [phenobarbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenobarbital "Phenobarbital") pills.

The police discover the French couple at the hotel registered as "Mr. and Mrs. Julien Tavernier" and find Julien's car and gun next to the Benckers' corpses and Julien's raincoat in their stolen Mercedes. They search Julien's office, escorted by the security guard, and discover Simon's body. Once the building's power is switched back on, Julien escapes from the elevator and goes to a cafe, unaware that he has been identified as a murder suspect in the morning newspapers. He is arrested and charged with the murder of the Benckers, unable to convince the police that he was trapped in the elevator all weekend. The rope he left attached to the balcony eventually falls loose on its own.

Florence obtains Véronique's address from the florist and finds Véronique and Louis still alive. She accuses the drowsy couple of murdering the Benckers and calls the police with an anonymous tip. Louis believes he's gotten away with the murder when he sees Julien's picture in the paper, but Véronique reminds him of the roll of film. Louis rushes to the motel's photo lab, tailed by Florence, and is arrested on the spot. Inside the lab Commissaire Cherrier shows Florence the photos of her and Julien that have been developed and are now evidence against them. Cherrier informs Florence she will probably get a harsher sentence than Julien, and Florence replies she did it for love and believes she will one day be reunited with Julien.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

This low-budget black-and-white production was 24-year-old Louis Malle's first feature film. He had previously worked with [Jacques Cousteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Cousteau "Jacques Cousteau") for several years, and was credited as co-director of the documentary _[The Silent World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silent\_World "The Silent World")_ (1956).

Malle cast [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau") after seeing her in the Paris stage production of [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams")' _[Cat on a Hot Tin Roof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat\_on\_a\_Hot\_Tin\_Roof "Cat on a Hot Tin Roof")_. She had already been in a number of films, but her role in this film is often considered her breakthrough. Malle filmed her without the heavy makeup and extreme lighting that previous directors had demanded. Scenes of Moreau wandering down the [Champs Elysees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champs_Elysees "Champs Elysees") at night were shot on fast film from a baby carriage using only available light from the street and shop windows.

## Soundtrack

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Soundtrack")]

Main article: [Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (soundtrack)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascenseur_pour_l'%C3%A9chafaud_(soundtrack) "Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (soundtrack)")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg)

Jazz trumpeter [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), who produced an innovative score for _Elevator to the Gallows_, pictured in 1956.

[Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s score for the film is considered by many to be groundbreaking,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-romina-3) with jazz critic Phil Johnson describing it as "the loneliest trumpet sound you will ever hear, and the model for sad-core music ever since. Hear it and weep."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-4)[Richard Brody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Brody "Richard Brody"), film critic and writer for _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_, wrote in 2016 that the score itself is "better than the film, by far".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

### Recording

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recording")]

In 1957, Davis, an already well known and highly regarded jazz performer and composer, received an invitation to perform in a three-week tour of Europe as a solo artist. Davis had just abandoned his "[first great quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#First_Great_Quintet/Sextet_(1955%E2%80%9358) "Miles Davis Quintet")" of 1955–56, including saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), due to their addiction to heroin. He was beginning to try and live a healthier life, although he was still using cocaine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989209-6) Additionally, Davis, during his time performing, had been experiencing an immense amount of racism and enjoyed the chance to leave the United States for a while.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7)

Marcel Romano, promoter and jazz enthusiast, picked Davis up from the airport in November 1957 with the initial intention of telling him he would feature in a film about jazz.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7) However, this plan fell through before Davis even arrived. Instead, film technician Jean-Claude Rappeneau, whom Romano had hired for the project, mentioned that he had been working on a feature film with young director Louis Malle who had an interest in jazz music.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7) Romano told Davis about the film and said Davis seemed interested in the project, so they organised a private screening for him. Davis took notes, asking questions about the relationships between the characters and explanations of the plot. He later wrote in his autobiography that he agreed to the job because he had never written music for a film before and it would be "a great learning experience".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989217-8)

While touring Europe, Davis asked that a piano be brought to his hotel room. Over the next two weeks, he began to improvise some themes that would be used in the film.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5) Davis chose to use musicians he had been performing with on his European tour: saxophonist [Barney Wilen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barney_Wilen "Barney Wilen"), pianist [René Urtreger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Urtreger "René Urtreger"), bassist [Pierre Michelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Michelot "Pierre Michelot") and drummer [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke"). They had only been informed about the project a couple of days prior and went into the session unprepared, having not even seen the film.

On 4 December 1957 at 10 p.m., Davis and his band went to the Le Poste Parisien studios to record the score. The band drank together for an hour, played for four hours, then took two hours of editing, and left the studio by 5 a.m. the next day having finished the film score.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-9)

### Analysis and influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Analysis and influence")]

The soundtrack features eight of Davis's extended improvisations, all recorded in the four-hour session. The only song mapped out in detail was "Sur L'Autoroute", and Davis gave minimal instructions to the band for the rest of the soundtrack. He gave them two chordal structures, D minor and C seventh chords, and they improvised around these.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-Allmusic-10) Scales rather than chords took precedence, maintaining harmonic simplicity and fragmenting the themes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7) Michelot said in a 1988 interview, "What characterised the session is the absence of a defined theme."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

The mood of the soundtrack is described as generally "dour and somber",[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-Allmusic-10) but the pace is picked up on tracks such as "Dîner au Motel". The songs "Générique" and "L'Assassinat de Carala" feature Davis's distinctive trumpet style that is echoed through dire straits or death wish motifs.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-Allmusic-10) Phil Johnson further described the soundtrack as a "powerfully expressive, highly concentrated, freely inspired performance".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

The scoring process for _Elevator to the Gallows_ was a milestone event in the development of Davis's theory of [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5) Modal jazz became highly influential in the late '50s and '60s, switching from the chorally dense sound of [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"). Davis opened up a new gateway between composition and improvisation in this soundtrack, a pathway which he would explore in the 1959 modal jazz album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind\_of\_Blue "Kind of Blue")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-UDiscoverMusic-7) This style of music would influence not only future jazz musicians but the sound of film noir itself. Richard Brody highlights this in his article, writing, "The use of jazz and jazz-derived soundtracks became so predominant, that jazz came to seem like the natural backdrop for high-speed chases, mass mayhem, and cold-blooded murder, because the films for which jazz players were enlisted were uniformly violent."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

## Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elevator_to_the_Gallows&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Critical response")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Identite-LouisMalle-1958-Sacem.png/250px-Identite-LouisMalle-1958-Sacem.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Identite-LouisMalle-1958-Sacem.png)

Malle in 1958

For _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_, journalist [Barry Farrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Farrell_(journalist) "Barry Farrell (journalist)") wrote:

> Moreau had 20 forgettable films behind her. ... Malle put Moreau under an honest light and wisely let his camera linger. The film was nothing special, but it did accomplish one thing: it proposed a new ideal of cinematic realism, a new way to look at a woman. All the drama in the story was in Moreau's face—the face that had been hidden behind cosmetics and flattering lights in all her earlier films. When Malle [made] _[The Lovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lovers\_(1958\_film) "The Lovers (1958 film)")_ the following year, it was obvious who his woman would be. For one thing, he had discovered her, and for another, they were in love.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-11)

In a review of the film's 2005 theatrical re-release, [Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") observed that Moreau's face when Florence is pondering Julien's whereabouts "is often illuminated only by the lights of the cafes and shops that she passes; at a time when actresses were lit and photographed with care, these scenes had a shock value, and influenced many films to come." He further argued that Louis and Véronique were a precursor to the young couple in [Jean-Luc Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Godard "Jean-Luc Godard")'s _[Breathless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathless\_(1960\_film) "Breathless (1960 film)")_ (1960).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-12) In a 2016 article, _[New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_ film critic [Richard Brody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Brody "Richard Brody") claimed the film is more important for its place in French film history than for its own artistic merits, with the exception of Davis's score, which he said "is worth hearing entirely on its own. It's better than the film itself, by far, and there are better ways to hear it than in the movie—namely, by listening to a CD that features the entire studio sessions from which the score was edited."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-The_New_Yorker-5)

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film holds an approval rating of 93% based on 60 reviews, with an average rating of 8.30/10. The website's critics consensus reads, "Louis Malle's hypnotic debut is a noir with genuine soul, infusing its tale of best laid plans gone awry with wistful performances, swooning cinematography, and a sultry soundtrack."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-13)[Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 94 out of 100, based on 16 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows#cite_note-14)

**Peter Miller** (born 1968) is a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian "Canadian")[actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor "Actor").

His credits have included the television series _[MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MVP\_(TV\_series) "MVP (TV series)")_, _[Virginie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginie "Virginie")_ and _[Lance et Compte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lance\_et\_Compte "Lance et Compte")_, and the films _[Mambo Italiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo\_Italiano\_(film) "Mambo Italiano (film)")_[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-1) and _[Rouge sang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Storm\_Within\_(2013\_film) "The Storm Within (2013 film)")_. Miller portrayed [Galeazzo Maria Sforza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeazzo_Maria_Sforza "Galeazzo Maria Sforza") in the 2009 short-film series _[Assassin's Creed: Lineage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassin's\_Creed:\_Lineage "Assassin's Creed: Lineage")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-2)

Miller graduated from the [Neighborhood Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhood_Playhouse "Neighborhood Playhouse") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). He was born in [Chibougamau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chibougamau "Chibougamau"), [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") and spent part of his childhood in the [Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas "Bahamas"). His mother is of [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") descent and his father is of [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") descent. He is [anglophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language")-[francophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francophone "Francophone") bilingual.

He is also a former professional football player in the [Canadian Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Football_League "Canadian Football League"). He was drafted in the seventh round of the [1992 CFL draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_CFL_draft "1992 CFL draft") by the [Saskatchewan Roughriders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan_Roughriders "Saskatchewan Roughriders") and played six seasons in the CFL with the Roughriders, [BC Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BC_Lions "BC Lions"), and [Toronto Argonauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Argonauts "Toronto Argonauts") as a [linebacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linebacker "Linebacker"); he played [college football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football "College football") for [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Tigers_football "Pacific Tigers football").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Miller_(actor)#cite_note-3)
